Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 1:

(Surat al-'Ankabut)

Makkiyyah (Meccan), though it is said to be Madaniyyah (Medinan). It is also said that from its beginning up to the end of the tenth verse it was revealed in Mecca and the rest in Medina, or that up to the end of the tenth verse it was revealed in Medina and the rest in Mecca, or the reverse. It has either seventy or sixty-nine verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and that they will not be tested?﴾

The first issue: concerning the connection of the beginning of this surah with what precedes it, and there are several aspects to this:

The first: When God the Exalted said before this surah: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained upon you the Qur'an will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾, and what was meant by it was that He would return him to Mecca, dominant, overcoming the disbelievers, victorious and seeking vengeance, and this entailed bearing the hardships of fighting, which was difficult for some, God the Exalted said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe"﴾, and will not be commanded to strive (jihad).

The second aspect: When God the Exalted said at the end of the previous surah: ﴿And invite to your Lord﴾, and in inviting to Him there was spear-thrusting, swords and striking, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, and his companions were commanded to strive if the disbelievers did not believe merely by invitation, this was difficult for some, so He said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone﴾.

The third aspect: When God the Exalted said at the end of the previous surah: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, He mentioned after it what nullifies the claim of those who deny the Resurrection, so He said: ﴿To Him is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning: not everything perishes without return, rather everything that perishes has a return to God.

Having made this clear, know that those who deny the Resurrection say: there is no benefit in obligations, for they are hardships in the present and have no benefit in the future, since there is no future or return after destruction and cessation, so there is no benefit in them.

So when God made clear that they will be returned to Him, He made clear that the matter is not as they supposed, but rather the imposition of obligation is good, so that He may reward the grateful and punish the ungrateful. So He said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone﴾ without being obligated, without any action by which they return to their Lord.

The second issue: concerning the wisdom of opening this surah with letters of the alphabet (huruf al-tahajji). Let us first present a general statement on the opening of surahs with letters, so we say: when the Wise addresses one who is heedless or whose mind is occupied with some concern, he places before the intended speech something else, so that the addressee is drawn by it and turns his heart toward it, and then he proceeds to the intended matter.

Having established this, we say: that which precedes the intended matter may be speech with a comprehensible meaning, like the speaker's saying "Listen," "Pay attention to me," or "Be with me." It may be something that has the sense of meaningful speech, like the saying "Is it Zayd? O Zayd! Ala, O Zayd!" It may be a sound without meaning, like one who whistles behind a person to make him turn. It may be a sound made without the mouth, as a person claps his hands so that the listener turns to him.

Furthermore, the more complete the heedlessness and the more important the intended speech, the more there is of what precedes the intended matter. For this reason the one who is near is called with the hamzah, so one says "Is it Zayd?", the distant one is called with "ya," so one says "O Zayd!", and the heedless one is first alerted, so one says "Ala, O Zayd!" Having established this, we say: although the Prophet, peace be upon him, was alert of mind, he was a human being whom one matter occupies away from another, so it was fitting for the Wise to place before the intended speech letters that serve as alerts. Moreover, when those letters do not have a comprehensible meaning, they are more effective in achieving the intended purpose, which is alerting, than letters that have a meaning; for when the placing of letters is meant to draw the listener's attention to the speaker to hear what follows, if that preface is a composed utterance and an intelligible statement, then when the listener hears it, he may think that it is the whole of the intended matter and that there is no further speech after it, and so he stops giving attention.

But if he hears from him a sound without meaning, he remains attentive to it and does not withdraw his gaze from it until he hears something else, because he is certain that what he heard is not the intended matter. Therefore, placing letters that have no meaning in their conventional usage before the intended speech contains a profound wisdom. If someone asks: what is the wisdom in the particularity of some surahs with these letters?

We say: the human intellect is incapable of grasping individual things in their details, and God knows all things best, but we mention what God grants us success in. We say: every surah that begins with letters of the alphabet also mentions in its opening the Book, or the Revelation, or the Qur'an, such as God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿That is the Book﴾ (al-Baqarah: 1); ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾ (Al 'Imran: 1-3); ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ ﴿A Book sent down to you﴾ (al-A'raf: 1-2); ﴿Ya, Sin﴾ ﴿By the Qur'an﴾ (Ya Sin: 1-2); ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an﴾ (Sad: 1); ﴿Qaf, by the glorious Qur'an﴾ (Qaf: 1); ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ (al-Sajdah: 1-2); ﴿Ha, Mim﴾ ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 1-2), except three surahs: ﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad﴾ (Maryam: 1); ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿Do people think﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 1); ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ (al-Rum: 1). The wisdom in opening the surahs in which there is the Qur'an, the Revelation, or the Book with letters is that the Qur'an is great, its revelation is weighty, and the Book bears a burden, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We will charge you with a weighty word﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 5). Every surah that begins with mention of the Qur'an, the Book, or the Revelation has placed before it an alert that makes the addressee attentive to listen. One cannot say that every surah is Qur'an and that listening to it is listening to the Qur'an, whether or not it contains explicit mention of the Qur'an, so it was necessary that every surah begin with an alert. Also, there are surahs containing mention of the revelation and the Book with no letters placed before them, such as God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾ (al-Kahf: 1); His saying: ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾ (al-Nur: 1); His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion﴾ (al-Furqan: 1); and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Decree﴾ (al-Qadr: 1).

Our answer to the first is: there is no doubt that every surah is part of the Qur'an, but the surah in which there is mention of the Qur'an and the Book, although it is part of the Qur'an, alerts to the whole Qur'an; for God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Ta Ha﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you﴾ (Ta Ha: 1-2), although it is only part of the Qur'an, contains mention of the whole Qur'an, so its example is like the example of a book that comes from a king to his subject in which there is some task, and another book that comes from him to him in which it says: "We have written to you a book containing Our commands, so comply with them." Without doubt the burden of the second book is greater than the weight of the first.

As for the second, [the surahs such as] ﴿Praise be to God﴾ and ﴿Blessed is He who﴾ are intended glorifications, and a servant does not neglect the glorification of God, so it does not need an alert, unlike commands and prohibitions. As for mention of the Book in them, it is to describe the greatness of the One to whom the glorification belongs. ﴿A surah which We have sent down﴾: we have already explained that it is part of the Qur'an, and it contains mention of its sending down; but in the surah we mentioned there is mention of the whole Qur'an, so it is greater in the soul and weightier.

* * *

As for God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ (al-Qadr: 1), we say: this does not come upon a mind occupied with something else, as is evident from the fact that it mentions a pronoun in it, and a pronoun refers to a previously mentioned or known antecedent, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾, the pronoun refers to something known to the Prophet, peace be upon him, so he was already alert to it and so was not alerted.

Know that alerting has occurred in the Qur'an through means other than letters whose meaning is not understood, as in God the Exalted's saying: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ (al-Hajj: 1); His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear God﴾ (al-Ahzab: 1); ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit﴾ (al-Tahrim: 1), because these are awesome, great matters, for fearing God as He truly deserves to be feared is a great matter, so the call that is used for the distant and heedless was placed before them as an alert. As for this surah, it is opened with letters and does not begin with the Book or the Qur'an, and that is because the Qur'an's weight and burden lie in what it contains of obligations and meanings, and this surah contains mention of all the obligations, where He said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe"﴾, meaning: they will not be left alone merely by that, but they will be commanded with kinds of obligations. Thus the meaning found in the surahs that mention the Qur'an, which comprises commands and prohibitions, is found here.

If it is said: a similar statement with a similar meaning occurs in the surah of al-Tawbah, God the Exalted's saying: ﴿Or do you think that you will be left alone, while God has not yet known those among you who strove﴾ (al-Tawbah: 16), and the letters of the alphabet were not placed before it. We say: the answer to this is quite clear, namely that this is the beginning of a speech; that is why the interrogation was with the hamzah, He said ﴿Do you think﴾. That is the middle of a speech, as evidenced by the interrogation occurring with "am" (or). The alert occurs at the beginning of speech, not in its middle. As for ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ (al-Rum: 1-2), it will come in its place, God willing. This is the complete discussion on the letters.

**The third issue: the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of *Alif Lam Mim* (﴿الم﴾).** The full discussion has already been given in Surah al-Baqarah, along with the views transmitted on its interpretation. Here we add to what was said there: letters have no i'rab (grammatical inflection), because they function as attention-calling sounds.

**The fourth issue: the occasion of revelation of these verses.** There are several reports:

The first: they were revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and Salama ibn Hisham, who were being tortured in Makkah.

The second: they were revealed concerning groups in Makkah who emigrated, and the disbelievers pursued them. Some of them were martyred and the rest were saved.

The third: they were revealed concerning Mahja ibn Abdullah, who was killed on the day of Badr.

**The fifth issue: the interpretation.** His saying ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone﴾ means: do they suppose that they will be left alone merely by saying ﴿"We believe"﴾, while ﴿they will not be tested﴾, that is, they will not be tried with the bodily and financial obligations?

The grammarians differed concerning His saying ﴿that they say﴾. Some said: "that they will be left alone" is governed by "that they say", i.e., "that they will be left alone by saying." Others said: "that they will be left alone" is followed by "they say, 'We believe'." The apparent meaning of the first view is that they are prevented from saying "We believe," as is understood from the statement of a speaker, "You think you are left alone from hitting Zayd," meaning you are prevented from that. This is far-fetched, because Allah does not prevent anyone from saying "I believe." Rather, the intended meaning of this commentator is that they are not left alone saying "We believe" without being tested, so they are prevented from this whole matter by the imposition of obligations upon them.

**The sixth issue: the spiritual benefits.** The ultimate purpose of creation is worship, and the highest goal in worship is the attainment of the love of Allah, as occurs in the report: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through worship until I love him." Whoever's heart is more filled with the love of Allah is greater in rank before Allah. However, the heart has an interpreter, which is the tongue, and the tongue has confirmers, which are the limbs, and these confirmers have purifiers. So when a person says "I believe" with his tongue, he has claimed the love of Allah in his heart, and so he needs witnesses. When he employs his limbs in carrying out what the edifice of faith is built upon, he obtains confirming witnesses for his claim. When he expends his self and his wealth in the way of Allah, and purifies his deeds by abandoning all else, he purifies those witnesses who confirmed what he said. Thus his name is written in the registers of the lovers, and his share is established among the categories of those brought near. To this refers His saying: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone for saying, "We believe"?﴾, meaning: do they suppose that their claim will be accepted without witnesses, and their witnesses without purifiers? Rather, all of this is necessary so that they may be among the lovers.

**A second benefit:** The lowest rank of the servant is that he be a Muslim, for what lies below it is the levels of disbelief. Islam is the first rank attained by the servant. When he attains this station, his name is recorded and his share is confirmed. However, those employed by kings are of various kinds. Among them is one who is diligent in his task and proceeds in his work, so he is transferred from one service to a service higher than it in rank. Among them is one who is lazy and falls behind, so he is transferred to a service lower than it. Among them is one who is left in his task without change, and among them is one whose record is cut off and whose name is erased from the registers. Likewise, among the servants of Allah, the Muslim may be a worshipper who turns devotedly to worship, accepted for felicity, so he is transferred from the rank of the believers to the rank of the certain, which is the rank of those brought near. And among them is one who performs little obedience and is occupied with dissolute conduct, so he is transferred to a rank below it, the rank of the disobedient and the station of the hard-hearted. Sometimes he belittles his faults and magnifies his sins, so he leaves worship deprived and joins the people of obstinacy, stoned. And among them is one who remains at the first level of Paradise, and they are the simple-minded.

So Allah, giving good tidings to the obedient and diligent, says: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone﴾, meaning: do they suppose that they will be left at the first stations? No, rather they will be transferred to the highest ranks, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge, [Allah will raise] by degrees﴾ (al-Mujadila: 11), and ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their selves over those who sit back by a degree﴾ (al-Nisa': 95).

And to the opposite, to the lazy, He said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone for saying, "We believe"?﴾, meaning: if one says "I believe" and then lags behind through disobedience, he will be left alone and be content with that from him. No, rather he will be transferred to a lower station, which is the station of the disobedient or the disbeliever.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly tried those who came before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful, and He will surely make evident the liars.﴾

Allah mentioned what necessitates their consolation, so He said: "Thus did Allah deal with those before you, and He did not leave them merely at their saying 'We have believed,' but He prescribed upon them the acts of obedience and made them obligatory." Regarding His words ﴿Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: the saying of Muqatil, "Allah will surely see (fa-layarayanna Allah)."

The second: "Allah will surely manifest (fa-layudhhirannah Allah)."

The third: "Allah will surely distinguish (fa-layumayyizannah Allah)." The upshot according to this is that the exegetes thought that taking the verse according to its apparent meaning necessitates the renewal of Allah's knowledge, whereas Allah knows the truthful and the liar before the testing. So how can it be said that He knows it at the time of testing? We say: the verse is to be taken according to its apparent meaning, because Allah's knowledge is an attribute in which everything that actually occurs is manifested as it occurs. Before the imposition of obligations, Allah knew that Zayd, for example, would obey and 'Amr would disobey; then at the time of the imposition and the carrying out, He knows that the one is obedient and the other disobedient; and after the carrying out, He knows that the one has obeyed and the other has disobeyed, and His knowledge does not change in any of these states. What changes is the known.

We illustrate this with an example from the sensible realm, and to Allah belongs the highest similitude: a clear, polished mirror, hung from some place and facing a direction, which is not moved; then Zayd passes before it wearing a white garment, and Zayd appears in it in a white garment; and when 'Amr passes before it in a yellow garment, he appears in it likewise. Does it occur to anyone's mind that the mirror has changed in its being iron, or that it has altered in its roundness, or that its understanding has differed in its polish, or that it has moved from its inhabitants? None of these things occurs to anyone, and one is certain that what changes is what passes in front of it. Understand this.

Allah's knowledge is like this example, or rather higher than this example, for the mirror is capable of change while Allah's knowledge is not capable of that. So His words ﴿Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful﴾ mean: it occurs from one whom Allah knows will perform the obedience, so He knows that he is obedient by that knowledge. ﴿And He will surely make evident the liars﴾ means: whoever says "I am a believer" and was truthful when the acts of worship were imposed, that becomes manifest from him and is known; and whoever says that while being a hypocrite is likewise made clear.

In His words ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in verb form, and His words ﴿the liars﴾ in the active participle form, there is a benefit, along with the fact that variation in wording is more indicative of eloquence. The active participle (ism al-fa'il) in many contexts indicates the establishment of the verbal noun (masdar) in the doer and its firm rootedness in him, whereas the past verb does not indicate this, as one says: "So-and-so drank wine" (shariba al-khamr) and "So-and-so is a drinker of wine" (sharib al-khamr); and "So-and-so's command was executed" (nafadha amruhu) and "So-and-so is one whose command is executed" (nafidh al-amr). The verb form does not convey repetition and firm rootedness, whereas the active participle conveys that. When this is established, we say: at the time of the revelation of the verse, the account concerned people who were recent in Islam at the beginning of the imposition of obligations and people who were persistent in disbelief and continuing upon it. So regarding the believers He said ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in verb form, meaning truthfulness was found in them; and regarding the disbeliever He said ﴿the liars﴾ in the form indicating permanence and continuity. For this reason He said ﴿On the Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:119) using the active participle form; because on the said Day, truthfulness may become firmly rooted in the heart of the believer, which is the Last Day, and this is not so at the beginning of Islam.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge.﴾

When He had explained the goodness of the obligation (taklif) through His saying: ﴿Do people think they will be left alone?﴾, He explained that whoever is charged with something and does not carry it out will be punished. Even if he is not punished at once, he will be punished in the future, and nothing escapes God, neither in the present nor in the outcome. This is a refutation of the view of those who say: the obligations are only guidance, and the threat attached to them is only encouragement and warning, and there is no punishment from God. Had He been punishing, He would not have been unable to punish immediately. Since He delays the punishment, He said: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us?﴾, meaning: it is not as they claim; rather, He punishes whom He punishes and rewards whom He rewards according to the ruling of promise and threat, and God does not break His promise. As for delay, it does not lead to neglect, and hastening the recompense of deeds is a concern of one who fears missing out, were it not for hastiness.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Evil is what they judge.﴾ Meaning: their judgment that they disobey and oppose God's command and will not be held to account is an evil judgment. A good judgment can only be the judgment of reason or the judgment of the Law (shar'). Reason does not judge that about God, for God may do what He wills, and the Law's ruling is contrary to what they claimed. So their judgment is a judgment of extreme badness and vileness.

Then He said: ﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

When He explained through His saying, "Do people think they will be left alone?", that the servant is not left without purpose in this world, and explained through His saying, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think...", that whoever abandons what he was charged with will be punished, He then explained that whoever acknowledges the Hereafter and works for it, his deed will not be lost and his hope will not be disappointed. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: We have mentioned in several places that the three foundations, namely: the first, which is God and His oneness; the other foundation, which is the Last Day; and the intermediate foundation, which is the Prophet sent from the first, connecting to the last, are hardly separated in the divine mention from one another. So His saying, "Do people think they will be left alone, that they will say 'We believe'?" contains an allusion to the first foundation, meaning: did they think that the first foundation suffices? His saying, "and they will not be tried" and "We certainly tried those before them" means by sending the messengers and clarifying the paths, and this contains an allusion to the second foundation. His saying, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think..." together with His saying, "Whoever hopes for the meeting with God" contains an allusion to the third foundation, which is the last.

The second issue: Some exegetes explained "the meeting with God" as seeing Him, and this is weak, for liqa' and mulaqah have the same meaning, and in the language it means arrival, so that if two inanimate things join, one has met the other.

The third issue: Some exegetes said that by hope (raja') is meant fear, and the meaning of "whoever hopes for the meeting with God" is "whoever fears God." This too is weak, for the well-known meaning of raja' is the expectation of good only, and because we agree that raja' is used in this sense: one says "I hope for God's bounty," and it is not understood from it "I fear God's bounty." Since it is used for this, it is not for anything else, to avoid ambiguity.

The fourth issue: The term of God (ajal Allah) may mean death, or it may mean the second life by resurrection. If it means death, this indicates the survival of souls after death, as reported in the traditions. This is because when one says, "Whoever hopes for good, the sultan is arriving," it is understood that what is connected with the arrival of the sultan is the good, so that if he arrives and the good is delayed, it is correct to say to the speaker: "Did you not say what you said and the sultan arrived, yet the good did not appear?" So if meeting did not occur at death, that would not be apt, as we mentioned in the example. And when this is clear, without survival there would be no meeting.

The fifth issue: His saying, "Whoever hopes," is a condition, and its consequent is "then the term of God is surely coming." What is conditioned on a condition is absent when the condition is absent, so whoever does not hope for the meeting with God would not have the term of God coming to him, and this is false. So what is the answer? We say: the mention of the coming of the term is meant as a promise to the obedient of what follows of reward, meaning: whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming with God's reward, and he is rewarded for his obedience in His presence. There is no doubt that whoever does not hope for it, the term of God does not come to him in a way that he is rewarded.

The sixth issue: He said, "and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and did not mention any other attribute such as the Mighty, the Wise, and others. This is because speech had preceded in His saying, "Do people think they will be left alone, that they will say," and action had preceded in His saying, "and they will not be tried," and in His saying, "So God will surely know those who are truthful," and in His saying, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think..." There is no doubt that speech is perceived by hearing, and action includes what is not perceived by sight and what is perceived by it, such as intentions, and knowledge encompasses both. He is the All-Hearing who hears what they say, and He is the All-Knowing who knows whoever is truthful in what he says from whoever lies. Also, He is All-Knowing who knows what they do, so He rewards and punishes. Here is a subtle point:

It is that the servant has three matters which are the categories of his good deeds:
The first: the work of his heart, which is assent (tasdiq), which is neither seen nor heard but only known; the work of his tongue, which is heard; and the work of his limbs and members, which is seen. When he does these things, God makes for what is heard from him what no ear has heard, and for what is seen from him what no eye has seen, and for the work of his heart what has never occurred to any human heart, as He described in the report about the description of Paradise.

The third issue: Some exegetes said that by hope (raja') is meant fear, and the meaning of "whoever hopes for the meeting with God" is "whoever fears God." This too is weak, for the well-known meaning of raja' is the expectation of good only, and because we agree that raja' is used in this sense: one says "I hope for God's bounty," and it is not understood from it "I fear God's bounty." Since it is used for this, it is not for anything else, to avoid ambiguity.

The fourth issue: The term of God (ajal Allah) may mean death, or it may mean the second life by resurrection. If it means death, this indicates the survival of souls after death, as reported in the traditions. This is because when one says, "Whoever hopes for good, the sultan is arriving," it is understood that what is connected with the arrival of the sultan is the good, so that if he arrives and the good is delayed, it is correct to say to the speaker: "Did you not say what you said and the sultan arrived, yet the good did not appear?" So if meeting did not occur at death, that would not be apt, as we mentioned in the example. And when this is clear, without survival there would be no meeting.

The fifth issue: His saying, "Whoever hopes," is a condition, and its consequent is "then the term of God is surely coming." What is conditioned on a condition is absent when the condition is absent, so whoever does not hope for the meeting with God would not have the term of God coming to him, and this is false. So what is the answer? We say: the mention of the coming of the term is meant as a promise to the obedient of what follows of reward, meaning: whoever hopes for the meeting with God, then the term of God is surely coming with God's reward, and he is rewarded for his obedience in His presence. There is no doubt that whoever does not hope for it, the term of God does not come to him in a way that he is rewarded.

The sixth issue: He said, "and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," and did not mention any other attribute such as the Mighty, the Wise, and others. This is because speech had preceded in His saying, "Do people think they will be left alone, that they will say," and action had preceded in His saying, "and they will not be tried," and in His saying, "So God will surely know those who are truthful," and in His saying, "Or do those who commit evil deeds think..." There is no doubt that speech is perceived by hearing, and action includes what is not perceived by sight and what is perceived by it, such as intentions, and knowledge encompasses both. He is the All-Hearing who hears what they say, and He is the All-Knowing who knows whoever is truthful in what he says from whoever lies. Also, He is All-Knowing who knows what they do, so He rewards and punishes. Here is a subtle point:

Page 29

It is that the servant has three matters which are the categories of his good deeds:
The first: the work of his heart, which is assent (tasdiq), which is neither seen nor heard but only known; the work of his tongue, which is heard; and the work of his limbs and members, which is seen. When he does these things, God makes for what is heard from him what no ear has heard, and for what is seen from him what no eye has seen, and for the work of his heart what has never occurred to any human heart, as He described in the report about the description of Paradise.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself. Indeed, Allah is free of need from the worlds.﴾

When He explained that the imposition of obligation is good and has occurred, and that for it there is a promise and a warning which nothing can repel, He explained that God's demanding that from the one under obligation is not for a benefit that returns to Him, for He is absolutely self-sufficient; there is nothing other than Him whose perfection depends upon it. Similar to this there is much in the Qur'an, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾ (Fussilat: 46), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own selves﴾ (al-Isra': 7). There are issues in this verse:

The first issue: The preceding verse together with this verse necessitates that the servant increase in righteous deeds and perfect them. That is because whoever does an act for the sake of a king, and knows that the king sees him and observes him, performs the deed well and perfects it; and when he knows that its benefit returns to him and is measured by the measure of his deed, he increases in it. So when God says, "Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing," the servant perfects his deed and makes it sincerely for Him; and when He says that his striving is for his own self, he increases in it.

The second issue: One may say: this indicates that reward is upon deeds, because when God, exalted is He, said, "Whoever strives, he strives only for himself," it is understood from it that whoever strives gains by his striving what he would not have gained without it. We say: it is so, but by the judgment of the promise, not by entitlement. Its explanation is that when God, exalted is He, explained that the one under obligation, if he strives, He rewards him, then when he does it, it is a striving beneficial to him, and there is no dispute about it. The dispute is only over whether God is obligated to reward for the deed apart from the promise, and it is not permissible for Him to show kindness to anyone except through deeds, and the verse contains no indication of this.

The third issue: His saying, "Innama" (indeed/only), implies restriction, so it should be that a person's striving is solely for himself, and no one else benefits from it. This is not so, for whoever strives benefits from it, and those whom he wishes to benefit; indeed, the parent and the child, by the blessing of the one who strives and his striving, both benefit. We say that this is a benefit to him, since the child's benefit is a benefit to the father. The restriction here means that his striving does not reach God such that any benefit comes to Him from it, and His saying, exalted is He, indicates this: ﴿Indeed, Allah is free of need from the worlds.﴾ On this there are issues:

The first: The verse indicates that taking what is best (al-aslah) is not obligatory upon God, because by the best He gains no benefit; otherwise He would be perfected by that benefit, which is other than Him and is from the world, so He would be perfected by other than Himself, and thus would be in need of it, whereas He is free of need from the worlds. Also, His acts are not caused by purposes, for the reasons we have explained.

The second: The verse indicates that He is not in a place, nor is He specifically upon the Throne, for it is from the world, and God is free of need of it, and one who is free of need of place cannot enter a place; because whatever enters a place is pointed to as being here or there in an independent manner, and what is pointed to as being here or there is impossible not to exist neither here nor there; otherwise reason would permit the perception of a body not in a place; and that is impossible.

The third issue: If someone says: His capability is not by a power, nor His worldliness by knowledge, otherwise He would, in His capability, be in need of a power which is other than Him, and everything other than Him is from the world, so He would be in need, whereas He is free of need. We say: Why do you say that His power is from the world? This is because the world is every existent apart from God with its attributes; that is, every existent that is outside the concept of the living God, the Capable, the Willing, the Knowing, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Speaker. Power is not outside the concept of the Capable, and knowledge is not outside the concept of the Knowing.

The fourth issue: The verse contains both good news and warning. As for the warning: since God is free of need from the worlds, if He destroys His servants with His punishment, there is nothing upon Him, because of His independence from them, and this necessitates great fear. As for the good news: since He is free of need, if He gave everything He created to one of His servants, there is nothing upon Him, because of His independence from it, and this necessitates complete hope.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely remove their misdeeds from them and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾

When He had stated in general terms that whoever does righteous deeds does so for his own self, He then stated in some detail, with a little elaboration, that the reward of the obedient, righteous person is his deed. So He said: ﴿Those who believe﴾. There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: It indicates that deeds are distinct from faith, because conjunction (ʿaṭf) necessitates difference.

The second issue: It indicates that deeds are included within what is intended by faith, because the removal of misdeeds and the reward with the best are contingent upon them, and they are the fruit of faith. An example of this is a fruitful tree: there is no doubt that its roots and branches are part of it, while the water that flows over it and the soil around it are not part of it; yet the fruit is not obtained except with that water and that external soil. Likewise, righteous deeds are with faith. Also, if harmful weeds and damaging thorns surround the tree, the fruit of the tree decreases; if they overpower it, the fruit is entirely lost and the tree is ruined. Likewise, sins act upon faith.

The third issue: Faith is affirmation (taṣdīq), as He said: ﴿And you would not believe us﴾ (Yūsuf: 17), meaning, you would not affirm us. In the usage of the Sharia, it is specifically restricted to affirmation of everything that God has said and that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has said, in detail when it is known in detail that it is the word of God or the word of the Messenger, or in general regarding what has not been known in detail. And the righteous deed, according to us, is everything that God has commanded; it becomes righteous by His command, and if He had forbidden it, it would not be righteous. Therefore, righteousness and corruption are not necessary attributes of the act itself. The Muʿtazila said that this is among the attributes of the act, and command and prohibition follow from it. Thus truthfulness is a righteous deed in itself, and God commands it for that reason. According to us, righteousness, corruption, goodness and ugliness follow from command and prohibition; according to them, command and prohibition follow from goodness and ugliness. The matter, in its full length, is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (kutub al-uṣūl).

صفحة ٣١
The fourth issue: The righteous deed remains, because the righteous (ṣāliḥ) is contrasted with the corrupt (fāsid), and the corrupt is that which is destroyed and perished. It is said: "the crops became corrupt" when they were destroyed or went out of the state of being useful, and it is said: "it is still righteous," meaning it remains in the condition it should be in. Once this is known, we say: the righteous deed does not remain by itself, because it is an accident (ʿaraḍ); nor does it remain by the agent, because the agent is perishing, as He said: ﴿Everything is perishing﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 88). Therefore its remaining must be through something that remains. But what remains is the Face of God, as He said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 88). So the deed should be for the Face of God, so that it may remain and thus be righteous. Whatever is not for His Face does not remain, neither by itself, nor by the agent, nor by the one for whom it is done, and so it is not righteous. Thus the righteous deed is that which the responsible person performs sincerely for God.

The fifth issue: This requires that intention be a condition for the righteous deeds, and it is the intention of performing the act for God. It includes the intention in fasting, contrary to Zufar, and in ablution, contrary to Abu Ḥanīfa, may God have mercy on him.

The sixth issue: The righteous deed is elevated, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the righteous deed raises it﴾ (Fāṭir: 10). However, it is not elevated except by the good word, for it ascends by itself, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ (Fāṭir: 10), and it elevates the deed. So the deed from one who is not a believer is not accepted. For this reason He placed faith before the deed. Here there is a subtle point: the deeds of the responsible person are three: the deed of his heart, which is his thinking, belief and affirmation; the deed of his tongue, which is his remembrance and testimony; and the deed of his limbs, which is his obedience and worship.

Bodily worship is not elevated by itself but is elevated by something else. The truthful word is elevated by itself, as was explained in the verse. The deed of the heart, which is thought, descends toward Him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God descends to the lowest heaven and says: Is there any repentant?" The repentant is one who regrets with his heart. Likewise His saying, peace be upon him: "God, mighty and majestic, says: I am with those whose hearts are broken," meaning through reflection on His weakness and My power, and his lowliness and My greatness. In terms of reason, whoever reflects on the blessings of God finds God, and his mind becomes present, and he knows that the deed of the heart reaches God; the deed of the tongue goes to God; and the deed of the limbs connects to God. This is an alert to the excellence of the deed of the heart.

The seventh issue: God mentioned two kinds of the servant's deeds: faith and righteous deed. And in return for them He mentioned two of His acts: the removal of misdeeds and the reward with the best, when He said: ﴿We will surely remove their misdeeds from them and We will surely reward them with the best.﴾ So the removal of misdeeds corresponds to faith, and the reward with the best corresponds to the righteous deed. This implies several matters:

The first: The believer will not be eternal in the Fire, because by his faith his misdeeds are removed, so he will not remain eternally in punishment.

The second: The best reward mentioned here is other than Paradise. This is because the believer by his faith enters Paradise, since his misdeeds are removed, and whoever has his misdeeds removed is admitted into Paradise. Therefore the best reward must be other than Paradise, namely that which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. It is not far-fetched that it is the vision (of God).

The third matter: Faith conceals the ugliness of sins in this world, so God conceals his faults in the Hereafter; and the righteous deed beautifies the state of the righteous in this world, so God rewards him with the best reward in the afterlife. Thus faith is not nullified by disobedience; rather, it overcomes sins, conceals them, and moves its possessor toward regret. And God knows best.

The eighth issue: His saying: ﴿We will surely remove their misdeeds from them﴾ requires the existence of misdeeds for them to be removed. ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ entirely—how could they have misdeeds? We answer: the response to this is from two aspects:

The first: promising a group something does not require promising each one of them each of those things. An example: if a king says to the people of a city: "If you obey me, I will honor your fathers, respect your sons, bestow favors upon you, and do good to you," this does not imply that he honors the fathers of those whose fathers have died, or respects the son of someone who has no son. Rather, its meaning is that he honors the father of whoever has a father, and respects the son of whoever has a son. Likewise, He removes the misdeed of whoever has a misdeed.

The second answer: There is no responsible person except that he has a misdeed. As for non-prophets, this is evident. As for the prophets, leaving what is better is, for them, like a misdeed for others. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿God pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ (al-Tawba: 43).

The ninth issue: His saying: ﴿and We will surely reward them with the best﴾ may have two meanings:

The first: We will surely reward them according to their best deeds.

The second: We will surely reward them with better than their deeds.

According to the first meaning, it means that We assess their deeds at their very best and reward them for them, not that He selects their best deed, rewards for it, and leaves the rest. According to the second meaning, it is close in meaning to His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ (al-Anʿam: 160), and His saying: ﴿he will have better than it﴾.

The tenth issue: He mentioned the state of the evildoer in general terms with His saying: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us?﴾, as an allusion to punishment in general terms.

And He mentioned the state of the doer of good in general terms with His saying: ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself﴾, and in detail with this verse, so that this would be an indication that His mercy is more complete than His wrath, and His grace is more comprehensive than His justice.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ There are several issues in this verse:

The first: What is the connection of this verse with what precedes it? We say: When Allah explained the goodness of the obligations and their occurrence, and explained the reward of one who fulfils the obligations, both their foundations and their branches, as an incentive for the responsible person to obey, He mentioned the obstacle and prevented him from choosing to follow it. So He said: If man submits to anyone, he should submit to his parents. Yet even if they command him to disobey, it is not permissible to follow them, let alone others. So let nothing prevent any of you from obeying Allah, and let no one follow anyone who commands disobedience to Allah.

The second issue: Regarding the recitation, it is recited as ḥusnan and iḥsānan. Ḥusnan is more apparent here. Whoever recites iḥsānan, it is from His saying: ﴿and to parents, kindness﴾ (al-Isra' 23). The explanation according to the well-known recitation is that Allah, may He be exalted, enjoined upon man that he do with his parents the goodness of courtesy in deed and word. Ḥusnan is indefinite to indicate perfection, as one says: "Zayd has wealth" (mālan).

The third issue: In His saying: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ there is evidence that following them in disbelief is not permissible. This is because kindness to parents became obligatory by the command of Allah, may He be exalted. So if the servant abandons the worship of Allah, may He be exalted, by the word of his parents, he has abandoned obedience to Allah, may He be exalted, and therefore does not submit to what He has enjoined upon him, and so he does not show kindness to his parents. Thus, following one's parents for the sake of kindness to them leads to abandoning kindness to them, and what its existence leads to its non-existence is invalid, so following is invalid. But if he refrains from association, he remains in obedience, and kindness to them is part of obedience, so he performs it. Thus, abandoning this kindness in form leads to kindness in reality.

The fourth issue: Kindness to parents is commanded, because they are the cause of the child's existence through birth, and the cause of his continuance through the customary upbringing; so they are a cause metaphorically, while Allah, may He be exalted, is the cause of him in reality through His will, and the cause of his continuance through restoration for happiness. Therefore He is more worthy that the servant treat Him well. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them.﴾ His saying: ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾ means that imitation (taqlid) in belief is not good, let alone imitation in disbelief. So when a person refrains from imitation in it, and does not obey without knowledge, he does not obey them at all; for knowledge of the soundness of their claim is impossible to attain. So when he does not associate by imitation, and associating with knowledge is impossible, then association never arises from him.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ That is: your end and your destination are to Me. Even if today you mix and associate with fathers, children, relatives and kin, there is no doubt that one who knows that his companionship with one is temporary and severed, while his presence before another is constant and never severed, will not abandon the pleasure of the one with whom his companionship endures for the pleasure of one who will leave him at another time.

Then His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so I will inform you﴾ contains a subtle point, namely that Allah, may He be exalted, says: Do not suppose that I am absent from you while your fathers are present, so that you agree with those present in the moment, relying on my absence and my lack of knowledge of your opposition to me. For I am present with you, knowing what you do, and I do not forget, so I will inform you of all of it.

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾. And in the verse there are several issues:

The First Issue: What is the benefit of repeating ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ a second time? We say: God, exalted is He, mentioned two categories of the responsible (mukallafun), the guided and the misguided, in His saying: ﴿So God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 3). He mentioned the state of the misguided in summary and the state of the guided in detail, in His saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾. When He had completed that, He mentioned two other categories, the guiding (hadi) and the misleading (mudill), so His saying: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ requires that he be guided by them. His saying: ﴿But if they strive with you to associate with Me﴾ is an explanation of their misguidance. His saying: ﴿To Me is your return, and I will inform you﴾ is, in summary, a warning to the misleader. His saying: ﴿Those who believe﴾ is in detail. He promised the guiding one, so He mentioned ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ once to explain the state of the guided, and once again to explain the state of the guiding one. What indicates this is that He said first: ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds﴾, and second: ﴿We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾. The righteous (al-salihun) are the guiding ones, because it is the rank of the prophets, and for this reason many of the prophets said: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 83).

The Second Issue: We have mentioned that the righteous deed (al-salih) remains, and the righteous people (al-salihun) remain, and their remaining is not by themselves but by their enduring deeds. So their deeds remain, and the one for whose sake they are done, which is the Face of God, remains, and the doers remain by the remaining of their deeds. This is contrary to worldly matters, for in this world the act remains by the agent, while in the Hereafter the agent remains by the act.

The Third Issue: It has been said regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾ that it means: We will surely admit them into the station of the righteous or into the abode of the righteous. The preferable view is that one should say: there is no need for an implied element; rather, He admits them among the righteous, i.e., He makes them of them and enrolls them in their number, just as one says: "The jurist is included among the scholars."

Page 34

The Fourth Issue: The philosophers said: the world of the elements is the world of generation and corruption, and whatever is in it is subject to corruption, for water departs from being water, decays, and air is generated from it. The world of the heavens has no generation or corruption in it, but it exists from non-existence, does not cease to exist, and the angel does not become dust, unlike the human, who becomes dust or something else. On this basis, the upper world is not corruptible, so it is righteous. Thus His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾ means: among the immaterial beings who have no corruption.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 10–11:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed, we were with you." Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And Allah will surely make evident those who believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites.﴾

We say: the categories of the responsible (mukallafun) are three: a believer who is apparent in the soundness of his belief; an unbeliever who openly proclaims his disbelief and obstinacy; and a wavering person between the two, who shows faith with his tongue and conceals disbelief in his heart. Allah, exalted is He, having clarified the two categories with His saying, ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 3), and having described their conditions with His saying, ﴿Do those who commit evil deeds think...﴾ up to His saying, ﴿and those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, then clarified the third category and said: ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: He said, ﴿says, "We believed"﴾ and did not say "I believed", even though He used singular verbs after it, as in His saying, ﴿when he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ and His saying, ﴿regards the trial of people﴾. That is because the hypocrite used to liken himself to the believer, saying, "My faith is like your faith." So He said, ﴿We believed﴾, meaning: I and the true believer believed, indicating that his faith is like theirs. This is like the case of a weak coward who goes out with the brave in battle and they defeat their enemies, and the coward says, "We went out, fought them and defeated them." It is valid for the listener to say to him: "And what were you among them, that you say 'we went out and fought'?" This objection shows that he understood from his words that his going out and fighting was like theirs, for it is not valid to deny him the claim of going out and fighting itself. Likewise, the saying of one who says, "I and the king found so-and-so and received him," is rejected, because what is understood from it is equality. So when they wanted to show that their faith was like the faith of the sincere ones, each one of them would say, ﴿We believed﴾, meaning: I and the sincere one.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿when he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ has the same meaning as His saying, ﴿and they were expelled from their homes and harmed for My cause﴾ (Al 'Imran: 195). However, the intended meaning of that verse is those who endured the harm of the disbelievers, while the intended meaning here is those who did not endure it. There He said, ﴿and were harmed for My cause﴾ (Al 'Imran: 195), and here He said, ﴿is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ and did not say "for the cause of Allah". The subtle point in this is that Allah intended to show the nobility of the patient believer and the baseness of the hypocrite and disbeliever. There He said that the believer was harmed "for the cause of Allah" so that he would abandon His path, but he did not abandon it. The hypocritical disbeliever was harmed and so he abandoned Allah by himself. He could have shown agreement with them if the harm reached the level of compulsion, while his heart remained at peace with faith, so he would not abandon Allah. Yet, despite this, he did not do so but abandoned Allah entirely. The believer was harmed and did not abandon the path of Allah; rather, he professed the two testimonies of faith and persevered in obedience and worship.

[Page 35]

The third issue: His saying, ﴿regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: he regards the trial of people as a deterrent from faith, just as the punishment of Allah is a deterrent from disbelief. It was also said that they panicked at the punishment of people just as they panicked at the punishment of Allah. In sum, its meaning is that they regarded the trial of people, despite its weakness and transience, as like the painful and lasting punishment of Allah, so that they hesitated in the matter and said: "If we believe, we will be exposed to harm from people, and if we abandon faith, we will be exposed to what Muhammad (ﷺ) has threatened us with." They chose to avoid immediate harm. Hesitation occurs only when the two options are equal. And how can the torment of people be neither severe nor prolonged? For if the punishment is severe, like the punishment of Fire and others, the person dies immediately, so the torment does not last. And if it is prolonged, like imprisonment and confinement, it is not severe. But the punishment of Allah is severe and its duration is prolonged. Also, the punishment of people has a remedy, whereas the punishment of Allah has no remedy against it. Also, the punishment of people brings great reward for the one who endures it, whereas after the punishment of Allah there is only painful punishment. Hardship that leads to great comfort is pleasant and is not counted as punishment, just as a harmful growth is cut out and is not counted as punishment.

The fourth issue: He said, ﴿the trial of people﴾ and did not say "the punishment of people", because the act of the servant is a test and examination from Allah. The trial of him is that some people are empowered over the one who has professed the word of faith in order to harm him, so that his rank becomes evident, just as He made the obligations a test and examination. This indicates that enduring the calamity that comes from people is a test and examination from Allah, just like enduring the acts of worship.

The fifth issue: If someone says: This implies preventing the believer from uttering the word of disbelief under compulsion, because whoever utters the word of disbelief under compulsion to avoid immediate punishment would have made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah. We say: That is not the case. Because the one who is compelled to disbelieve while his heart is at peace with faith has not made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah. For the punishment of Allah requires abandoning what one is punished for, both outwardly and inwardly. This compelled believer has not made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah, in such a way that he abandons what he would be punished for outwardly and inwardly; rather, faith remains within him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed, we were with you."﴾ That is, the custom of the hypocrite is that if he sees power in the hands of the disbelievers, he displays what he conceals, shows companionship, and claims to be a follower. There are benefits in this, which we mention in issues:

The first issue: He said, ﴿And if victory comes from your Lord﴾ and did not say "from Allah", even though everything mentioned before was with the mention of Allah, as in His saying, ﴿is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ and His saying, ﴿like the punishment of Allah﴾. That is because "Rabb" (Lord) is a name whose specific signification is compassion and mercy, while "Allah" is a name whose signification is awe and greatness. So at the mention of victory He used the word that signifies mercy and tenderness, and at the mention of punishment He used the word that signifies greatness.

The second issue: He did not say, "if it comes to you" or "if it comes to you (singular)", but said: ﴿And if victory comes from your Lord﴾. If victory came to them, they would not say, ﴿Indeed, we were with you﴾. This implies that they would be saying, "We are with you" whenever victory comes, whether it comes to them or to the believers. We say: this statement implies that they would be saying "We are with you" when victory comes. But victory comes only to the believer, as Allah said: ﴿And it is incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾ (al-Rum: 47). Also, the dominance of the disbeliever over the Muslim is not victory, because victory is that whose outcome is sound. The evidence is that if one of two armies is defeated at the outset, then the defeated army rallies once more and defeats the victors, the name "victorious" is applied only to the one who has the final outcome. Likewise for the Muslim: even if he is broken at the moment, the final outcome belongs to the God-fearing, so victory is theirs in reality.

The third issue: Regarding (﴿لَيَقُولُنَّ﴾, "they will surely say"), there are two readings:

One of them is with a fatha (on the nun, as "layaqulanna"), taking it as referring back to His saying, ﴿those who say, "We believed"﴾; that is, the one who says "We believed" abandons that statement when he is harmed, and when victory comes he says, "Indeed, we were with you."

The second is with a damma (as "layaqulunna"), using the plural, attributing the saying to all the people indicated by the implied meaning, since the hypocrites were a group. Then Allah, exalted is He, clarified that they intended deception, and this is not valid for them, because deception occurs only when the speech contradicts the heart. The listener builds the matter on their speech and does not know what is in their heart, so the matter is confused for him. But as for Allah, exalted is He, He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts, and He knows better than a man what is in another man's breast, so the matter is not confused for Him. This indicates that the consideration is what is in the heart. So the hypocrite who shows faith and conceals disbelief is a disbeliever, and the believer who is compelled, who shows disbelief and conceals faith, is a believer. And Allah knows best what is in the breasts of the worlds. Since He clarified that He knows what is in the hearts of the worlds, He clarified that He knows the sincere believer even if he does not speak, and the hypocrite even if he speaks. So He said: ﴿And Allah will surely make evident those who believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites.﴾ Its explanation has already preceded, but there is one issue in it: Allah said there, ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful﴾, and here He said, ﴿And Allah will surely make evident those who believed﴾. We say: since the mention there was of the believer and the disbeliever, and the disbeliever in his saying is a liar, for he says, "Allah is more than one", while the believer in his saying is truthful, for he used to say "Allah is one", and there was no mention there of one who conceals the opposite of what he shows, the outcome there was two categories: truthful and liar. Here, the hypocrite was truthful in his saying, for he used to say "Allah is one", so He considered the matter of the heart regarding the hypocrite and said: ﴿and He will surely make evident the hypocrites﴾, and He considered the matter of the heart regarding the believer, which is affirmation, and said: ﴿And Allah will surely make evident those who believed﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 10–11:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah. And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, "Indeed, we were with you." Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of the worlds?﴾ ﴿And Allah will surely make evident those who believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites.﴾

We say: the categories of the responsible (mukallafun) are three: a believer who is apparent in the soundness of his belief; an unbeliever who openly proclaims his disbelief and obstinacy; and a wavering person between the two, who shows faith with his tongue and conceals disbelief in his heart. Allah, exalted is He, having clarified the two categories with His saying, ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 3), and having described their conditions with His saying, ﴿Do those who commit evil deeds think...﴾ up to His saying, ﴿and those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, then clarified the third category and said: ﴿And among the people is he who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: He said, ﴿says, "We believed"﴾ and did not say "I believed", even though He used singular verbs after it, as in His saying, ﴿when he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ and His saying, ﴿regards the trial of people﴾. That is because the hypocrite used to liken himself to the believer, saying, "My faith is like your faith." So He said, ﴿We believed﴾, meaning: I and the true believer believed, indicating that his faith is like theirs. This is like the case of a weak coward who goes out with the brave in battle and they defeat their enemies, and the coward says, "We went out, fought them and defeated them." It is valid for the listener to say to him: "And what were you among them, that you say 'we went out and fought'?" This objection shows that he understood from his words that his going out and fighting was like theirs, for it is not valid to deny him the claim of going out and fighting itself. Likewise, the saying of one who says, "I and the king found so-and-so and received him," is rejected, because what is understood from it is equality. So when they wanted to show that their faith was like the faith of the sincere ones, each one of them would say, ﴿We believed﴾, meaning: I and the sincere one.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿when he is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ has the same meaning as His saying, ﴿and they were expelled from their homes and harmed for My cause﴾ (Al 'Imran: 195). However, the intended meaning of that verse is those who endured the harm of the disbelievers, while the intended meaning here is those who did not endure it. There He said, ﴿and were harmed for My cause﴾ (Al 'Imran: 195), and here He said, ﴿is harmed for the sake of Allah﴾ and did not say "for the cause of Allah". The subtle point in this is that Allah intended to show the nobility of the patient believer and the baseness of the hypocrite and disbeliever. There He said that the believer was harmed "for the cause of Allah" so that he would abandon His path, but he did not abandon it. The hypocritical disbeliever was harmed and so he abandoned Allah by himself. He could have shown agreement with them if the harm reached the level of compulsion, while his heart remained at peace with faith, so he would not abandon Allah. Yet, despite this, he did not do so but abandoned Allah entirely. The believer was harmed and did not abandon the path of Allah; rather, he professed the two testimonies of faith and persevered in obedience and worship.

[Page 35]

The third issue: His saying, ﴿regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: he regards the trial of people as a deterrent from faith, just as the punishment of Allah is a deterrent from disbelief. It was also said that they panicked at the punishment of people just as they panicked at the punishment of Allah. In sum, its meaning is that they regarded the trial of people, despite its weakness and transience, as like the painful and lasting punishment of Allah, so that they hesitated in the matter and said: "If we believe, we will be exposed to harm from people, and if we abandon faith, we will be exposed to what Muhammad (ﷺ) has threatened us with." They chose to avoid immediate harm. Hesitation occurs only when the two options are equal. And how can the torment of people be neither severe nor prolonged? For if the punishment is severe, like the punishment of Fire and others, the person dies immediately, so the torment does not last. And if it is prolonged, like imprisonment and confinement, it is not severe. But the punishment of Allah is severe and its duration is prolonged. Also, the punishment of people has a remedy, whereas the punishment of Allah has no remedy against it. Also, the punishment of people brings great reward for the one who endures it, whereas after the punishment of Allah there is only painful punishment. Hardship that leads to great comfort is pleasant and is not counted as punishment, just as a harmful growth is cut out and is not counted as punishment.

The fourth issue: He said, ﴿the trial of people﴾ and did not say "the punishment of people", because the act of the servant is a test and examination from Allah. The trial of him is that some people are empowered over the one who has professed the word of faith in order to harm him, so that his rank becomes evident, just as He made the obligations a test and examination. This indicates that enduring the calamity that comes from people is a test and examination from Allah, just like enduring the acts of worship.

The fifth issue: If someone says: This implies preventing the believer from uttering the word of disbelief under compulsion, because whoever utters the word of disbelief under compulsion to avoid immediate punishment would have made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah. We say: That is not the case. Because the one who is compelled to disbelieve while his heart is at peace with faith has not made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah. For the punishment of Allah requires abandoning what one is punished for, both outwardly and inwardly. This compelled believer has not made the trial of people like the punishment of Allah, in such a way that he abandons what he would be punished for outwardly and inwardly; rather, faith remains within him.
