Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." And they will not bear anything of their sins. Indeed, they are liars.﴾

When Allah the Exalted had explained the three groups and their conditions, and mentioned that the disbeliever calls the one who says "I have believed" back to disbelief through trial, and explained that the punishment of Allah is greater than it, and the disbeliever would say to the believer: "Why do you endure humiliation and harm? Why do you not ward off humiliation and punishment from yourself by agreeing with us?" then the answer of the believer would be to say: "Out of fear of the punishment of Allah, on account of the sin of your creed." So they said: "There is no sin in it, and if there is sin in it, then it is upon us." And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: (ولْنَحْمِلْ) (wa-l-naḥmil, "and let us bear") is in the form of a command, and the one commanded is other than the one who commands. So how is it valid to command oneself from the person? We say: the form is a command, but the meaning is a condition and a consequence, i.e., "if you follow us, we will bear your sins." The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf) said: it is in the sense of the speech of one who wants two commands to be united in existence, so he says: "Let there be giving from you, and let there be supplication from me." So his saying (ولنحمل), meaning "let there be bearing from us," is not in reality a command of request and obligation.

The second issue: He said: ﴿And they are not bearers of anything of their sins﴾, and after this He said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾.

Here He negated the bearing, and there He affirmed the bearing, so how is the reconciliation between them? We say: the saying of the speaker, "So-and-so bore from so-and-so," indicates that the burden of so-and-so was lightened; and if his burden was not lightened, then he has not borne anything from it. Likewise here: "they are not bearers of anything of their sins," meaning they do not remove a sin from them, while they bear burdens because of their misguiding others, and they bear burdens because of their own error, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever establishes a bad practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it, without that diminishing anything from their burden."

The third issue: the form is a command, and a command does not admit of truth or falsehood, so how is His saying ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾ to be understood? We say: it has been made clear that its meaning is a condition and a consequence, so it is as if they said: "If you follow us, we will bear your sins." And they lied in this, for they will not bear anything.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens, and burdens along with their burdens; and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to fabricate.﴾

Regarding what they used to fabricate, it may have three meanings:

First: Their saying ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ was uttered on the basis of their belief that there is no sin in disbelief. Then on the Day of Resurrection the opposite of that will become apparent to them, and they will be questioned about that fabrication.

Second: Their saying ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ was based on the belief that there is no gathering (resurrection). So when the Day of Resurrection comes, the opposite of that will become apparent to them, and they will be questioned and it will be said to them: Did you not say that there is no gathering?

Third: When they said: "If you follow us, we will bear your sins on the Day of Resurrection," it will be said to them: "Then bear their sins," and they will not be able to bear them, so they will be questioned, and it will be said to them: "Why did you fabricate?"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 14–15:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is as follows. When God, exalted is He, explained the obligations (taklif), mentioned the categories of those who are obligated, promised the truthful believer a great reward, and threatened the disbelievers and hypocrites with painful punishment, and He had mentioned that this obligation is not restricted to the Prophet and his companions and his community, so that it would be difficult for them, but that before him it was also so, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly tested those who were before them﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 3), He mentioned among those whom He obligated a group: among them Noah, the Prophet, upon him be peace, and his people, and among them Abraham, upon him be peace, and others. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years.﴾ And in the verse there are issues:

The first issue: What is the benefit in mentioning the duration of his stay? We say: The Prophet, upon him be peace, used to feel distress in his chest because of the disbelievers not entering Islam and their persistence in disbelief. So (God) said: Noah remained approximately a thousand years in calling (his people), and only a few of his people believed, and he was patient and did not grow weary. So you are more worthy of patience because of the shortness of the duration of your stay and the abundance of the number of your community. Also, the disbelievers used to be deceived by the delay of the punishment from them for longer; and despite that they were not saved. So with this measure of delay, they should not be deceived, for the punishment will overtake them.

The second issue: Some scholars said: The exception in a number is a statement of what remains. So when a speaker says: "I owe so-and-so ten less three," it is as if he said: "I owe seven." Given this, His saying ﴿a thousand years less fifty years﴾ is like His saying: nine hundred and fifty years. So what is the benefit in deviating from this expression to another? We say: al-Zamakhshari said that there are two benefits in it:

The first: that the exception indicates precision, and leaving it may be thought to indicate approximation. For whoever says: "So-and-so lived a thousand years," it may be imagined that he means: a thousand years approximately, not precisely. So when he says "less a month" or "less a year," that supposition is removed and precision is understood from it.

The second: that the mention of Noah's stay among his people was to show that he endured much patience. So the Prophet, upon him be peace, is more worthy of patience despite the shortness of the duration of his calling. And if that is so, then mentioning the number in the highest of the number-levels that have a singular, established name is appropriate, for the levels of numbers are the units up to ten, the tens up to a hundred, the hundreds up to a thousand, and after that the multiplication is by repetition, so it is said: ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and a million.

The third issue: Some physicians said: the human lifespan does not exceed one hundred and twenty years, and the verse indicates the opposite of their view, and reason agrees with it. For the persistence of the composition found in the human being is possible in its essence, otherwise it would not remain; and the continued effect of the agent upon it is possible, because if its agent is necessarily existent, its permanence is evident; and if it is other than that, then it has an agent, which ends at the Necessary, and He is everlasting, so His effect may be everlasting. Therefore persistence is possible in its essence. If it does not occur, it is due to an impediment; but the impediment is possibly non-existent, otherwise this measure would not have remained, because the existence of the impeding accident would be necessary. Thus it is clear that their statement is contrary to reason and transmission. (Then we say:) There is no dispute between us and them, for they say: the natural lifespan does not exceed one hundred and twenty years, and we say: this lifespan is not natural, rather it is a divine gift; as for the natural lifespan, it does not last for us even for an instant, let alone a hundred years or more.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾

In this there is an indication to a subtle point: that God does not punish merely for the existence of wrongdoing, for otherwise He would punish whoever wronged and repented, since wrongdoing did proceed from him. Rather He punishes for persistence in wrongdoing. So His saying ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾ means: He destroyed them while they were upon their wrongdoing, and had they abandoned it He would not have destroyed them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship, and made it a sign for the worlds.﴾

Regarding the referent of the pronoun in His saying ﴿and made it﴾, there are two possibilities:

One: that it refers to the ship mentioned. On this view, regarding its being a sign there are several aspects:

One of them: that it was built before the water appeared, and had it not been for God's informing Noah and His announcing it to him, he would not have occupied himself with it, and salvation would not have been achieved for them.

Second: that Noah was commanded to take along a group of people and a quantity of provisions, and the great sea is not expected by anyone to recede; then the water receded before the provisions ran out, and had that not happened salvation would not have been achieved. So it was by God's grace, not merely by the ship.

Third: that God, exalted is He, ordained the ship's safety from disturbing winds and harmful creatures, and had that not been so, salvation would not have been achieved.

The second: that it refers to the event or to the salvation, i.e., We made the event or the salvation a sign for the worlds.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 16:

Page 39

Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people, "Worship God and fear Him. That is better for you, if you only knew."﴾

When he (al-Razi) finished pointing to the narrative of Noah, he mentioned the narrative of Abraham. Regarding "Abraham" there are two readings:

The first: the accusative (naṣb), which is the well-known one.

The second: the nominative (raf'), in the sense of: "And among the messengers is Abraham."

As for the first, it has two possible analyses:

The first: that it is in the accusative governed by a verb not mentioned, which means: "He mentioned Abraham."

The second: that it is in the accusative governed by what is mentioned, namely His saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent﴾. So it is as if He said: "And We sent Abraham." On this basis, there are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: His saying ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is an adverbial clause (ẓarf) modifying "We sent," meaning: "We sent Abraham when he said to his people." However, His saying ﴿to his people, "Worship God"﴾ is a call (da'wah), and sending (irsal) occurs before the call, so how can His saying "And We sent Abraham when he said to his people" be understood, given that he would already be a messenger before it? We answer this in two ways:

The first: that sending (irsal) is an ongoing matter, so at the time of his saying "to his people, Worship God," he was a messenger. This is like the speaker who says: "We stood for the amir when he came out of the house," though standing may have occurred before the coming out; but because the standing extended up to that time, it is valid.

The second way: Abraham, by merely God's guidance to him, knew the corruption of the polytheists' statement, and he was guiding them to right conduct before the sending. When he was occupied with calling to Islam, God Exalted sent him. His saying ﴿Worship God and fear Him﴾ is an allusion to monotheism (tawhid), since tawhid is affirming God and negating other than Him. So His saying ﴿Worship God﴾ alludes to affirmation, and His saying ﴿and fear Him﴾ alludes to negation of others; for whoever associates with the King another in his kingdom has committed the greatest of crimes. It is also possible to say: ﴿Worship God﴾ alludes to performing the obligations, and ﴿and fear Him﴾ alludes to abstaining from the prohibitions. Under the first falls acknowledgment of God, and under the second, refraining from association. Then His saying ﴿That is better for you, if you only knew﴾ means: the worship of God and fearing Him is better, and the matter is so, because opposing the worship of God Exalted is nullification (ta'til), and opposing fear of Him is association (tashrik), and both are evil, rationally and by consideration. As for reason: the possible (mumkin) must have a cause that is not itself possible, definitively, to avoid an infinite regress (tasalsul), and this is the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud), so there is no nullification, since we have a God. As for association, its invalidity is rational, and that its opposite is better, namely: the partner of the Necessary, if he is not necessary, how can he be a partner? And if he is necessary, it entails two necessary beings, which share in necessity and differ in divinity, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, so composition is entailed in both, and thus they are not two necessary beings, because they are composite, and so nullification is entailed. As for consideration: nobility would not be a king or near a king, yet a human is not a king of the heavens and earths, so the highest of his ranks is to be near the King. But nearness comes through worship, as God Exalted said: ﴿And prostrate and draw near﴾ (al-'Alaq: 19), and He said: "The approachers will never draw near to Me with anything like the performance of what I have obligated upon them," and He said: "The servant does not cease drawing near to Me through worship." So the one who nullifies is neither a king nor near a king, since he does not believe in a King, so he has no rank at all. As for association, whoever has a master who has no equal is higher in rank than one whose master has base partners. Thus whoever says "My Lord, nothing is like Him" is higher in rank than whoever says "My master is a carved idol, powerless like himself." It is established that the worship of God and fearing Him is good, and it is good for you, that is, good for people, if they know the proofs and considerations we have mentioned.

[Page 40]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You worship only idols apart from Allah, and you invent a lie.﴾

He mentioned the falsity of their doctrine in the most eloquent manner. This is because the one who is worshipped is worshipped for one of several reasons. Either he deserves worship in his own essence, like a slave who serves his master who bought him, whether the master feeds him from hunger or keeps him from sleep. Or he is beneficial in the present, like one who serves another for a benefit that the other conveys to him, such as the hired worker for wages. Or he is beneficial in the future, like one who serves another while expecting something from him in the future. Or the one worshipped is feared by the worshipper. Ibrahim said: ﴿You worship only idols apart from Allah,﴾ indicating that they do not deserve worship for their own sake, since they are idols that possess no honour.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those whom you worship apart from Allah do not possess for you any provision. So seek provision from Allah, worship Him, and be grateful to Him. To Him you will be returned.﴾

This indicates the absence of benefit both in the present and in the final outcome. This is because benefit is either in existence or in continuance. But there is no benefit from them in existence, because their existence comes from you, since you shape them and carve them. And there is no benefit in continuance, because that is by provision, and provision does not come from them. Then He explained that all of that is obtained from Allah, saying: ﴿So seek provision from Allah.﴾ His words ﴿Allah﴾ indicate that He deserves worship in His essence, and His words ﴿provision﴾ indicate that benefit is obtained from Him, both immediately and in the future. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: He said ﴿do not possess for you any provision﴾ in indefinite form (nakirah, the indefinite noun), and said ﴿seek provision from Allah﴾ in definite form (ma'rifah, the definite noun). What is the benefit of this? We say: al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Do not possess for you any provision﴾ is indefinite in the context of negation, meaning that there is no provision with them at all. And he said: it is definite in affirmation: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning all provision is with Him, so seek it from Him. There is another aspect: provision from Allah is known through His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ (Hud: 6). Provision from the idols is not known, so He said: ﴿do not possess for you any provision,﴾ because no knowledge of it is obtained. And He said: ﴿So seek from Allah the provision﴾ that was promised. Then He said: ﴿and worship Him,﴾ meaning worship Him because He deserves worship in His essence. ﴿And be grateful to Him,﴾ meaning because He precedes the blessings by creation and continues them by provision. ﴿To Him you will be returned,﴾ meaning worship Him because He is the place of return from which good is expected, and not otherwise.

Then God, Exalted, said: ﴿And if you deny, then communities before you have denied, and the Messenger's duty is only to convey clearly.﴾

When He had finished explaining monotheism (tawhid), He followed it with a warning, saying: ﴿And if you deny﴾. Regarding the addressees in this verse there are two views:

The first: they are the people of Abraham. The verse is a report about the people of Abraham, as if Abraham said to his people: ﴿And if you deny, then communities before you have denied﴾, and I have done what is incumbent upon me of conveying the message, for the Messenger has no duty except conveying and making clear.

The second: it is an address to the people of Muhammad (ﷺ). Its rationale is that most narratives are told for specific purposes, but the purpose is forgotten because of the pleasantness of the narration; for this reason the narrator often says, "Why did I tell this story?" The Prophet (ﷺ) intended to remind his people of the condition of those who passed before, so that they would refrain from denial and be deterred out of fear of punishment. Thus, in the course of relating their story, he said: "O my people, if you deny, then peoples before you have denied and were destroyed. If you deny, I fear for you what befell others."

On the first view, there are several issues:

The first issue: How is His saying ﴿then communities have denied﴾ to be understood, given that before Abraham there was only the people of Noah, who were a single community? The answer to this has two aspects:

The first: before Noah there were peoples, such as the people of Idris, and the people of Shith and Adam.

The second: Noah lived for a thousand years and more, and a generation would die while its children came after it, and the fathers would enjoin the sons to refrain from following [the prophets]; so the people of Noah alone suffice as "communities."

The second issue: What is meant by ﴿conveying (al-balagh)﴾ and ﴿clear (al-mubin)﴾? We say: conveying is the mention of the matters, and making clear is the establishing of proof for them.

The third issue: The verse indicates that delaying clarification beyond the time of need is not permissible, because if the Messenger conveys something and does not clarify it, then he has not brought a clear conveyance, and so he has not fulfilled what is incumbent upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 19:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation, then repeats it? Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ When He had explained the first foundation, which is Tawhid (oneness of God), and alluded to the second foundation, which is prophethood, by His saying: ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾, He began to explain the third foundation, which is the Resurrection (hashr). We have mentioned many times that these three foundations are hardly separated from one another in the divine discourse; wherever God mentions two of them, He mentions the third.

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: When did a person see the beginning of creation, such that it is said: ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation﴾? We say: the intended meaning is clear knowledge that is like sight. The intelligent person knows that the beginning is from Allah, because the first creation cannot come from a created thing; otherwise the first creation would not be a first creation. Thus it is from Allah. This is if we say that the intended meaning is establishing creation itself. If we say that the intended meaning of "beginning" is the first creation of the human being, and "repetition" is his creation a second time, then we say: the intelligent person cannot fail to know that the creator of himself is none other than a Powerful, Wise One who shapes children in the wombs and creates him from a drop of semen with the utmost perfection and firmness. That which was created first is an evident, manifest thing, so the word "sight" is applied to that knowledge, and He said: ﴿Have they not seen﴾, meaning: Do they not know with a clear, evident knowledge ﴿how Allah originates creation﴾, creating him from dust, gathering him from dust, and likewise gathering his parts from the dust and breathing His spirit into him. Indeed, it is even easier for you, for one who carves stones and places one thing beside another and then something separates them, says: placing one thing beside another in this instance is easier for me, because the stones are already carved, and it is known that any one of them is fit to be placed beside another. On this manner the speech of Allah came in His saying: ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾ (Ar-Rum: 27), and to this is the allusion in His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾.

The second issue: He said: ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation﴾. He linked the seeing to the how (kayfiyyah), not to the creation itself. Why did He not say: "Have they not seen that Allah created, or originated creation?" And is the how not unknown? We say: this degree of the how is known, namely that He created him when he was not a thing mentioned, and that He created him from a drop which is from nourishment, which is from water and dust. This degree is sufficient for attaining knowledge of the possibility of repetition, for repetition is like it.

The third issue: Why did He say: ﴿Then He repeats it. Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾, bringing out His name a second time, and not say: "Indeed, that is easy for Him," as He said: "Then He repeats it" without bringing out the name? We say: with the establishment of proof that it is easy, He emphasized it by manifesting His name, for this also necessitates knowledge that it is easy. When a person hears the word "Allah" and understands its meaning, that He is the Living, Powerful with complete power, that nothing overcomes Him, the Knowing with all-encompassing knowledge of the atoms of every body, whose will is effective and whose decree none can repel, he is certain of the possibility of repetition.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation; then Allah will bring forth the final creation. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent."﴾

The preceding verse was an allusion to intuitive knowledge (al-'ilm al-hadsi), which is what is attained without seeking. So He said ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ in the form of a question, meaning to deem its absence unlikely. In this verse He said: if this knowledge has not been attained by you, then reflect upon the horizons of the earth so that you may know through discursive knowledge (al-'ilm al-fikri). This is because human beings have degrees of comprehension: some grasp a thing without instruction or the establishment of a proof for it; some do not understand except through explanation; and some do not understand it at all. So He said: if you are not of the first category, then travel through the earth, that is, direct your thinking through the earth and turn your minds over the events outside yourselves, so that you may know the beginning of creation. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: In the first verse He used the expression "seeing" (ru'yah), and in this one "looking" (nazar). What is the wisdom in this? We say: intuitive knowledge is more complete than discursive knowledge, as has been made clear, and seeing is more complete than looking, because looking leads to seeing. One says: "I looked and I saw," and that which leads to a thing is other than that thing. So He said in the first case: if you have not attained seeing, then look upon the earth so that seeing may be attained by you.

The second issue: He mentioned this verse in the imperative form, and in the first verse in the interrogative form, because if intuitive knowledge is attained, then commanding it is commanding what is already attained; and if it is not attained, it is not attained except through seeking, because through seeking the intuitive becomes discursive, so commanding it would be imposing what cannot be borne. As for discursive knowledge, it is within capacity, so the command to it was revealed.

The third issue: He made the name of Allah explicit in the first verse at the beginning, where He said: ﴿how Allah originates creation﴾, and kept it implicit at the repetition. In this verse He kept it implicit at the beginning and made it explicit at the repetition, where He said: ﴿then Allah brings forth﴾. This is because in the first verse the name of Allah had not been preceded by a verb to which the beginning could be attributed, so He said: ﴿how Allah originates﴾, then He said: ﴿then He repeats it﴾, as the speaker says: "Zayd struck 'Amr, then struck Bakr," and does not need to make Zayd's name explicit, being satisfied with the first mention. In the second verse the mention of the beginning was attributed to Allah, so He sufficed with it and did not make it explicit, like the speaker's saying: "Have you not known how Zayd went out? Hear from me how he went out," without making Zayd's name explicit. As for making it explicit at the second instance of origination, where He said: ﴿then Allah brings forth﴾, although it would have sufficed to say: "then He brings forth the final creation," this is for a far-reaching wisdom, which is what we have mentioned: that with the establishment of proof for the possibility of the return, He made the name explicit, so that whoever understands the One named by it, with the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty, will be certain of the permissibility of the return. So Allah, making it explicit and manifest, so that there may fall upon the human mind from His name the perfection of

Page 43

His power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and the penetration of His will, and he acknowledges the occurrence of His beginning and the permissibility of His return. If it is said: why did He not say: "then Allah repeats it," for the same wisdom and benefit you have mentioned? We say, for two reasons:

One of them: that Allah was explicit and manifest at close proximity, in His saying: ﴿how Allah originates creation﴾, and there was nothing between them except the word "creation." Here, however, He was not mentioned at the beginning, so He made Him explicit.

The second: that the proof here was complete for the permissibility of the return, because the proofs are confined to the horizons and to the souls, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ (Fussilat: 53). In the first verse He pointed to the psychological proof attained by this human being from himself, and in the second verse He pointed to the proof attained from the horizons by His saying: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth.﴾ When both proofs were complete, He emphasized it by making His name explicit. As for the first proof, He emphasized it by the second proof, so He did not say: "then Allah repeats it."

The fourth issue: In the first verse He mentioned it in the future form, saying: ﴿Have they not seen how He originates﴾, and here He said in the past form, saying: ﴿then look how He began﴾, and did not say "how He begins." We say: the first proof is the psychological proof which necessitates intuitive knowledge, and it in every state necessitates knowledge of the beginning of creation. So He said: if you do not have knowledge that Allah in every state originates a creation, then look at the created things so that you may attain knowledge that Allah began a creation, and the purpose is attained from this measure, for He will bring it forth as He began that.

The fifth issue: In this verse He said ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, and in the first verse He said ﴿Indeed that is for Allah easy﴾. In this there are two benefits:

The first: that the first proof is the psychological proof, and although its necessitation is complete intuitive knowledge, yet with the joining of the proof of the horizons to it, general knowledge is attained, because by looking into himself he knew himself, his need of Allah, and his existence from Him, and by looking at the horizons he knew the need of others for Him and their existence from Him, so his knowledge was complete that everything is from Allah. So He said at the completion of mentioning the two proofs: ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, and said at the single proof: ﴿Indeed that﴾, that is, its repetition, ﴿for Allah is easy﴾.

The second: that we have shown that the first knowledge is more complete, even though the second is more general, and that a matter being easy for the agent is more complete than its being within his capacity, as evidenced by the fact that one who says of a man who carries a hundred (units) that he is capable of it, does not say that it is easy for him; but when asked about his carrying ten bushels, he says that this is easy for him. So we say: Allah the Exalted said: if you have not attained complete knowledge that these matters are easy and simple for Allah, then travel through the earth so that you may know that it is within capacity, and the mere fact that it is within capacity suffices for the possibility of the return.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 21–22:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿You cannot escape (Him) on earth or in the sky, and you have no protector or helper besides God.﴾

When He mentioned the Final Creation, He mentioned what will happen in it, namely the punishment of those who deny, as justice and wisdom, and the reward of those who turn back (to God), as grace and mercy. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: He mentioned the punishment before the mercy, even though His mercy precedes, as He (peace be upon him) said, reporting from Him: "My mercy precedes My wrath." We say this for two reasons:

The first: The preceding mention concerned the disbelievers, so He mentioned the punishment because the mention of those who deserve it had preceded, by way of the threat, and He followed it with mercy. Just as, after establishing the first principle, which is monotheism, He mentioned the threat in His saying: ﴿And if you deny, then nations have denied (before you)﴾, and they were destroyed by denial, so likewise, after establishing the other principle, He mentioned the threat by mentioning punishment. The mention of mercy came as a follow-up, so that punishment would not be mentioned alone. This confirms His saying: "My mercy precedes My wrath." This is because God, where the purpose was to mention punishment, did not single it out in the mention but mentioned mercy along with it.

The second issue: If He mentioned this to frighten the disobedient and gladden the believer, then had He said, "He punishes the disbeliever and has mercy on the believer," it would have been more effective in achieving the purpose. His saying ﴿He punishes whom He wills﴾ does not deter the disbeliever, since he may say, "Perhaps I will not be one whom God wills to punish." We say: this is more forceful in instilling fear, because God, by this, affirmed the enforcement of His will: when He wills to punish a person, no obstacle prevents Him. Then, it was known to the servants, by way of promise and threat, that He willed to punish the people of obstinacy, so complete fear arises from it. This is unlike if He had said, "He punishes the disobedient," for that does not indicate the completeness of His will, since it does not convey that if He willed to punish the believer, He would punish him. When this does not convey it, the disbeliever may say, "If my aim is not achieved in that case, it may be achieved in another case." Let us give him an example: If it is said that the king has the power to strike everyone in his lands, and he says, "Whoever opposes me, I will strike him," complete fear arises in the one who opposes him. But if it is said that he is able to strike the opponents and not able to strike the obedient, and he says, "Whoever opposes me, I will strike him," the opponent may imagine that he cannot strike such-and-such an obedient person, so he cannot strike me either, since I am like him. In this there is another benefit, namely general fear and general hope, because complete security from God brings about boldness, which leads to the obedient becoming disobedient.

The third issue: He said, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, although this matter has already been established and affirmed. Why did He repeat it? We say: When God mentioned punishment and mercy, and both may be immediate, He said, as it were: If that is delayed for you, do not think that it has been lost, for to Him is your return, upon Him is your reckoning, and with Him your reward and punishment are stored. For this reason He said after it, ﴿and you cannot escape (Him)﴾, meaning you cannot outrun God; rather, the return is to Him, and escape from Him is impossible. In the interpretation of this verse there are subtleties.

The first of them: It concerns the one being punished escaping the punishment, either by fleeing from it or by standing firm against it and resisting it in order to repel it. God mentioned both kinds, saying: ﴿You cannot escape (Him) on earth or in the sky﴾, meaning by fleeing: even if you ascended to the place of the Simak star in the sky, or descended to the place of the fish in the water, you would not leave the grip of God's power. So there is no hope of escaping by fleeing. As for standing firm, it is likewise, because escape is either by leaning on a strong support that intercedes, and which the one punishing cannot oppose, so the one punished slips away and the punisher is unable to reach him; or by seeking victory through a people who stand with him in repelling. Both of these are impossible, for you have no intercessor besides God, and no helper who repels. So there is no escape, neither by flight nor by standing firm.

The second: He said ﴿and you cannot escape (Him)﴾ and did not say "you do not make (Him) helpless" in the verbal form. This is because negating the act does not indicate negating the capacity. For whoever says "So-and-so does not sew" does not convey what is conveyed by his saying "He is not a tailor."

The third: He placed the earth before the sky, and the protector before the helper. This is because their possible flight is on earth; if any flight occurs from them, it will be on earth. Then, if we assume they had some other power, there would be ascent into the sky. As for repelling, a rational person who is able to repel by the most excellent means does not resort to anything else, and intercession is the most excellent. Moreover, there is no one among those present who does not have an intercessor who speaks on his behalf before a king, whereas not everyone has a helper who opposes the king on his behalf.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in His meeting—those have despaired of My mercy, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

When He had explained the two foundations, Tawhid (the oneness of God) and Resurrection (al-i'adah, the return), and had established them by proof, and had threatened those who opposed them in detail, He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in His meeting﴾, referring to the disbelievers in God, for indeed for Allah there is a sign in everything that indicates His oneness, so whoever associates partners with Him has disbelieved in the signs of Allah. It also refers to the denier of the gathering (al-hashr), for whoever denies it has disbelieved in the meeting with Allah. Then He said: ﴿those have despaired of My mercy﴾. When they associated partners, they removed themselves from the place of mercy, because one who has only a single source that meets his need is shown mercy, but when he has multiple sources, there remains no place for mercy. When they made for themselves gods, they did not acknowledge the need for a single determined path, so they despaired of the mercy of Allah. And when they denied the gathering and said, "There is no punishment," it was fitting that they be punished, to confirm the matter upon them. This is like a king who says, "I will punish whoever opposes me," and the one who denies him thinks he is far from him and says, "He cannot reach me." When he is brought before him, it is good for the king to punish him and to say, "Have I had power? Have I punished or not?" Thus it becomes clear that the absence of mercy suits association, and the painful punishment suits denial of the gathering.

Then, in the verse there are several benefits:

First: His saying ﴿those have despaired﴾, so that it indicates that people are restricted to them. He also said ﴿and those for them is a painful punishment﴾ for this reason. Had He said, "Those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and in His meeting have despaired of My mercy, and for them is a painful punishment," this benefit would not have been obtained. If someone says, "If He had been content with saying ﴿those﴾ once, it would have sufficed to convey what was mentioned," we reply: no, because if He had said, "those have despaired and for them is a painful punishment," someone might think that this combination is restricted to them, so the combination would exist only among them, while each one of the two could exist among others. But when He says, "those have despaired and those for them is a painful punishment," it conveys that each one is found only among them.

Second: When mentioning mercy, He attributed it to Himself, saying "My mercy," and when mentioning punishment, He did not attribute it to Himself, due to the precedence of His mercy, and to inform His servants of its generality for them and its necessity for Him.

Third: He attributed despair to them by His saying ﴿those have despaired﴾, thus forbidding it for them; had they hoped, He would have permitted it for them. If someone says, "What you mentioned of the correspondence between the two matters, despair and punishment, and the two matters, disbelief in the signs and disbelief in the meeting, implies that the painful punishment is not for one who disbelieves in Allah but acknowledges the gathering, or that despair is not for one who disbelieves in the gathering but believes in Allah," we say: the meaning of the verse is that they have despaired, and for them is an additional painful punishment because of their disbelief in the gathering. There is no doubt that punishment because of disbelief in the gathering applies only to one who disbelieves in the gathering. As for the other, one who disbelieves in the gathering is not a believer in Allah, because belief in Him is not valid unless one affirms what He has said, and the gathering is among that.

Then He said: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Page 46

When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had presented the three foundations and established the proof for them, the matter remained on their side: either a response, or the bringing of something that could serve as an answer to him. But they did not bring anything except their saying ﴿Kill him or burn him.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: How did He call their saying ﴿Kill him﴾ an answer, when it is not an answer? We say the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: It came from them in the manner of the speech of the arrogant, as a king says to the envoy of his adversary, "Our answer is the sword," although the sword is not an answer. Its meaning is: I will not counter him with an answer; rather I will counter him with the sword. Likewise they said: Do not answer his proofs, and kill him or burn him.

The second: Allah intended to show their misguidance, namely that they were mentioned in the context of an answer, this being what it is, though it is not an answer. Thus it became clear that they had no answer at all. This is because one who does not answer another and remains silent cannot be known to be unable to answer, since his silence may be due to inattention. But when one gives a corrupt answer, it is known that he intended to answer and was not able to.

The second issue: The ones who said "Kill him" are his people, and those commanded by their saying "Kill him" are also them; so the commander would be the same as the commanded? We say the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: Each one of them said to the others, "Kill him," so the command came from each one, and each one became one commanded, and there is no unity, because each one commanded the others.

The second: The answer is only given by the great and the leaders. When the notables of a town say something, it is said: "The people of the town agreed upon this," and the disagreement of the slaves and the lowly is not taken into account. Thus their answer, being that of their leaders, was that they said to their followers and helpers, "Kill him," because the answer is only issued by the great, and the killing is only carried out by the followers.

The third issue: Or is mentioned between two matters, the second of which is separable from the first, as one says: "Even or odd" (zawj aw fard), and one says: "This is a human or an animal," meaning that if he is not a human, then he is an animal. It is not correct to say: "This is an animal or a human," since it would be understood that he says he is an animal, and if he is not an animal, then he is a human, which is absurd. But burning includes killing; so His saying "Kill him or burn him" is like the saying of one who says: "An animal or a human." The answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: The usage contrary to what has been mentioned is common, and "or" (aw) is used in the place of "but rather" (bal), as one says: "I gave him a dinar or two dinars," and as one says: "Give him a dinar, but rather two dinars." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Stand up [to pray] the night, except a little, half of it, or reduce from it a little, or add to it﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 2–4). Likewise here: "Kill him, or add to the killing and burn him."

The second answer: We grant what you have mentioned, and the matter here is so, because burning is an act that leads to killing, and killing may fail to follow it. For one who throws another into the fire until his skin is entirely burned and he is taken out alive, it is correct to say: "So-and-so was burned, and so-and-so burned him, but he did not die." Likewise here they said: "Kill him, or do not hasten his killing, and torment him with fire; and if he withdraws his claim, let him go; and if he persists, let him be placed in the fire as his resting place."

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ The rational scholars differed about the manner of the deliverance. Some said: He made the fire cool, and this is the most correct, in agreement with His saying the Exalted: ﴿We said, "O fire, be cool and safe for Ibrahim."﴾ (al-Anbiya: 69). Some said: He created in Ibrahim a state by which he felt the fire to be cool. Some said: He left Ibrahim as he was and the fire as it was, and prevented the harm of the fire from him. All of these are possible, and Allah is capable of them. Some physicians denied all of them. As for stripping the fire of heat, they said: Heat in fire is essential, like evenness in four; it cannot separate from it. As for creating a state that cools the fire, they said: The human temperament has two extremes, excess and deficiency, so if it departs from them, the human would not remain human or would not live. For example, if the cold in the temperament is ten parts, he is human; if it becomes eleven, he is not human; if the cold parts are five, he remains human; but if they become four, he does not remain human. However, the coldness by which the fire is cooled is the temperament of the salamander, and if it occurred in a human he would die, or that would be so because the soul follows the temperament. As for the third, it is impossible that a piece of cotton be in the fire while the fire remains as it is and the cotton remains as it is and does not burn. We say: The verse is a refutation of them, and reason agrees with transmission. As for the first, it is on two grounds:

The first: Heat in fire admits of intensity and weakness, for the fire in charcoal, when blown upon, intensifies until it melts iron, and if not blown upon, it does not intensify. But weakness is the loss of some of the heat that was in the fire; so when the loss of some is possible, the loss of some other part of it is permissible, until it reaches a limit that does not harm the human. This is not so with evenness, for it neither intensifies nor weakens.

The second: In the principles of medicine it is mentioned that fire has a hot quality just as water has a cold quality; but we see that water loses its coldness and remains water. Likewise fire loses its heat and remains fire, a light that does not burn. As for the second, it is also possible, and their saying is refuted on two grounds:

The first: Denying their premise that the soul follows the temperament; rather Allah is capable of creating the human soul in a temperament like the temperament of ice.

The second: That we say, on your premise, no impossibility follows, because the quality we have described exists on the outer surface like a coating, and does not reach the heart and the principal organs. Do you not see that when a person touches ice for a time and then touches an ember, the fire does not affect his hand in burning it as it affects the hand of one who has taken his hand out of his pocket; and that is why his hand burns before this one's.

So if it is permissible for a quality to exist on the outer skin of a human that prevents the fire from burning it for a time, then it is permissible that this quality renew itself moment by moment, so that it does not burn.

As for the third: it is merely a claim of improbability, based on the absence of habitual experience; and we grant that this is not customary, because it is a miracle, and a miracle must be beyond the habitual course.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ That is, in His saving him from the fire there are signs. Here there are issues:

The first issue: Regarding the deliverance of Nuh and the people of the ark, He said: ﴿And We made it a sign﴾, and here He said: ﴿signs﴾ in the plural, because the deliverance by the ark is something that minds can comprehend; so there was no sign in it except through Allah's informing him of building it at the time of need, for had it not been for that, he would not have built it, lacking knowledge of what is hidden; and because Allah preserved the ark from destructive things like violent winds. As for the deliverance from the fire, it is marvelous, so He said "signs" concerning it.

The second issue: There He said ﴿a sign for the worlds﴾, and here He said ﴿for a people who believe﴾. He restricted the signs to believers, because the ark remained for years until people passed by it and saw it, so knowledge of it was attained by everyone; but as for the cooling of the fire, it did not remain, so it was not manifest to those after him except through the way of faith and assent. There is a subtle point in this: when Allah cooled the fire for Ibrahim because of his guidance in himself and his guiding of the children of his kind, and Allah had said to the believers that they have in Ibrahim a good example, there came to the believers good news that Allah would cool the fire upon them on the Day of Resurrection; so He said: Indeed in that cooling are signs for a people who believe.

The third issue: There He said ﴿And We made it﴾, and here He said "We made him" (ja'alnahu), because the ark did not become a sign in itself, and had Allah not created the flood, Nuh's act would have remained folly; so Allah the Exalted made the ark, after its existence, a sign. As for the cooling of the fire, it is in itself a sign once it exists, needing no other matter, like the creation of the flood, for it to become a sign.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he said, "You have only taken idols besides Allah as a bond of affection among you in the worldly life. Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and curse one another, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾

When Ibrahim came out of the fire, he returned to rebuking the disbelievers and explaining the corruption of what they were upon. He said: If I explain to you the corruption of your doctrine, and you have no answer and do not turn back from it, then this is nothing but imitation (taqlid, blind adherence). For among some of you and others there is affection, so none of you wants his companion to part from him in conduct and path. Or between you and your fathers there is affection, so you inherited them, took their sayings, and clung to their misguidance and ignorance. So His saying, ("You have only taken . . . . . . . . . affection among you"), means that this is not an argument at all. There is another aspect to it, a subtle investigation: it may be said that His saying, ("You have only taken . . . . . . affection among you"), means affection between the idols and their worshippers. That affection is this: the human being is composed of a body and an intellect. The body has bodily pleasures, and the intellect has intellectual pleasures. Whoever is dominated by physicality does not attend to intellectual pleasures, and whoever is dominated by intellectuality does not attend to bodily pleasures. This is like the madman when he needs to relieve a need, such as eating, drinking, or urinating, while he is among a group of notables in a gathering. He obtains what gives pleasure to his body, such as eating and urinating and other things, and does not attend to the intellectual pleasure of good conduct, praiseworthy qualities, and noble morals. The intelligent person bears bodily pain and attains intellectual pleasure, to the extent that if his expelling power overcomes his retaining power and a wind or a drop of water comes out of him, he nearly dies from shame and intellectual pain.

Given this established, they were feeble-minded, with physicality dominating them. Thus their intellects did not have room for a deity that is neither above them nor below them, neither to their right nor their left, neither in front of them nor behind them, and is not a body among bodies, nor anything that enters into imagination. They saw bodies suited to the dominant side in them adorned with jewels, so they loved them. Thus their taking of idols was an affection between them and the idols. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others﴾. That means: on the day when the blindness of hearts is removed and matters become clear to the discerning and the heedless, some of you will disavow others, and will know the corruption of what they were upon. The worshipper will say, "This is not my deity," and the worshipped will say, "These are not my worshippers." And some of you will curse one another. One will say to the other, "You caused me to be in punishment when you worshipped me," and the other will say, "You caused me to be in it when you misguided me by your worship." Each wants to distance his companion by cursing, yet they do not separate, but rather they are gathered together in the Fire as they were gathered together in this abode. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and your refuge will be the Fire﴾. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you will have no helpers﴾. That means: that Fire is not like your fire from which Allah saved Ibrahim and granted him victory. Rather, you are in the Fire and have no helper.

Here are some issues (masa'il, questions):

The first issue: Before this He said: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, in the singular form, whereas here He said in the plural form: ﴿and you will have no helpers﴾. The wisdom in this is that when they wanted to burn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, they said, "We shall support our gods," as Allah, exalted is He, related about them: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ (al-Anbiya': 68). So He said: You claimed that these have helpers, so what do you and they have, that is, the idols and their worshippers, of helpers? As for there, the claim of helpers had preceded from them, so He negated the category with His saying: ﴿nor a helper﴾.

The second issue: There He said: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, and here He did not mention the protector. We have explained that the meaning of "protector" (waliyy) is intercessor. That is: you have no intercessor and no repelling helper. Here, since the address included the idols, meaning "you, all of you," He did not say "intercessor," because they were all acknowledging that none of them has an intercessor, for they used to claim that their gods were intercessors, as He, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿These are our intercessors﴾ (Yunus: 18). An intercessor cannot have an intercessor of his own, so He did not negate the intercessor from them, since there was no need to negate what they acknowledged. As for there, the discourse was with them, and they used to claim that they had intercessors for themselves, so He negated it.

The third issue: There He said: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, which was expressed in the sense of an exception, so it is understood that they have a helper and protector, who is Allah, and that they have no protector or helper other than Him. Here He said: ﴿and you will have no helpers﴾ without an exception. We say: that was addressed with regard to their being in the world. So He said to them in the world: Do not think that you can overpower Allah, for no one has a helper for you. Rather, Allah, exalted is He, helps you if you repent. He is a helper prepared for you, whenever you want, you seek His help through repentance. This is the Day of Resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others﴾. The absence of a helper is general, because repentance on that day is not accepted. Whether they repent or do not repent, Allah does not help them, and they have no helper other than Him. So they have no helper absolutely.

[Page 49]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Lot believed in him, and [Abraham] said: "Indeed, I am a emigrant to my Lord."﴾ That is, to wherever He commanded me to turn toward. ﴿Indeed, He is the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ Almighty: He prevents my enemies from harming me by His might. Wise: He does not command me except with what accords with the perfection of His wisdom. And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿So Lot believed in him⦆ — that is, after he saw from him the overpowering miracle. Lot's rank was lofty, and his remaining until this time is something that diminishes from rank. Do you not see that Abu Bakr, when he accepted the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was of a luminous heart, accepted it before all others, without hearing the speech of the pebbles or seeing the splitting of the moon? So we say: Lot, when he saw his miracle, believed in his prophethood; as for the Oneness of God, he believed when he heard his good discourse. And to this He alluded with His saying: ﴿So Lot believed in him⦆, and He did not say "So Lot believed."

The second issue: How does His saying, ﴿And [Abraham] said: "Indeed, I am an emigrant to my Lord"⦆ connect to what came before? We say: when Abraham exerted himself in guidance and his people were not guided, and complete despair arose when they saw the greatest sign and did not believe, emigration became obligatory. For the guide who has guided his people and they have not benefited, his remaining among them is a corruption, because if he persists in guidance he is occupied with what yields no benefit while knowing it, and he becomes like one who says to a stone, "Be truthful," which is futile; or he remains silent, and silence is a sign of consent, so it is said that he has become one of us and is pleased with our deeds. And when there is no longer any reason for residence, emigration becomes obligatory.

The third issue: He said, ﴿an emigrant to my Lord⦆ and did not say "an emigrant to where my Lord commanded me," although emigration to the Lord suggests a direction. We say: His saying "an emigrant" to where my Lord commanded me is not, in sincerity, like His saying "to my Lord," because when a king issues a command for the troops to proceed to a certain place, and then one of them travels there for a purpose of his own, he has indeed emigrated to where the king commanded, but not sincerely for His sake. So he said, ﴿an emigrant to my Lord⦆, meaning: my turning toward the direction commanded for emigration is not seeking the direction; it is only seeking God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 27:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants, and We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾

We have already mentioned, in the interpretation (tafsir) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely remove from them their misdeeds and We will surely reward them﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 7), that the effect of God's mercy lies in two matters: security from the evil of punishment, and the bestowal of a good reward. This reaches the believer in the Hereafter with certainty, by the ruling of God's promise: the negation of punishment for him because he negated polytheism (shirk), and the affirmation of reward because he affirmed the One God. However, this is not necessarily attained in this world. For the disbeliever is often in comfort, while the believer goes hungry on his day and is anxious about his morrow. Yet both of these are sought in this world. As for averting immediate punishment, it is because there was reported in the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) his saying: "Protect us from the torment of poverty and the Fire." So the torment of poverty is an indication of averting immediate punishment. As for immediate reward, it is in His words: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ (al-Baqarah: 201).

With this established, we say: when Abraham (peace be upon him) first presented the declaration of God's oneness (tawhid), God averted from him the punishment of this world, which was the punishment of the Fire. When he presented it again and again, while the people persisted in denial and harmed him with torture, God gave him the other recompense, which is immediate reward, and enumerated it for him in His words: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾.

In the verse there is a subtle point: God changed all of Abraham's circumstances in this world into their opposites when the people wanted to torment him with fire, and he was solitary and alone. So God replaced his solitude with abundance, until he filled the world with his descendants. And when his people and near kin were initially astray and misguiding, among them Azar, God replaced his relatives with guided and guiding relatives, namely his descendants, in whom God placed prophethood and the Book. He was initially without status or wealth, and these two are the greatest worldly pleasures. God gave him his reward of wealth and status. His wealth increased until he had livestock whose number only God knows, to the point that it is said he had twelve thousand guard dogs with gold collars. As for status, it reached the point that blessing upon him is joined with blessing upon all the other prophets until the Day of Resurrection, and he became known as "the elder of the messengers" after having been obscure. Until one of them said: ﴿We heard a youth mentioning them, called Abraham﴾ (al-Anbiya': 60). This statement is said only about someone unknown among the people.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ That is, he does not have this only in this world, as is the case for one whose good deeds are repaid in this life, or who is given respite as a gradual lure so that he multiplies his misdeeds. Rather, this is for him a hasty benefit, and for him in the Hereafter there is the reward of guidance and messengership, which is his being among the righteous. For the servant's being righteous is the highest of his ranks. As we have explained, the righteous (salih) is one who remains in what is fitting, as one says: "The food is still good (salih)," meaning it remains in its proper condition. Whoever remains in what is fitting is not in punishment, and he has everything he desires of good reward.

There are two issues in the verse:

The first issue: Ishmael was among his righteous sons, and he had submitted to God's command to slaughter and yielded to God's judgment. Why then is he not mentioned? It may be said that he is mentioned in His words: ﴿and We placed prophethood among his descendants﴾, but his name was not stated explicitly, because the purpose was to show God's favour to Abraham through the gift of sons and grandsons. So He mentioned one of the sons, who was the eldest, and one of the grandsons, who was the most prominent. This is like one who says: "The sultan has among his servants kings and emirs, King so-and-so and Emir so-and-so," and does not enumerate them all, because mentioning that one is to explain the category, not his particular distinction. Had he mentioned others, it would have been understood as an enumeration and comprehensive inclusion of all, so one would assume that no others besides those named exist.

The second issue: God, exalted is He, placed prophethood among his descendants in answer to his supplication. A father ought to treat his two sons equally. How then did prophethood come to be more among the descendants of Isaac than among the descendants of Ishmael? We say: God, exalted is He, divided the time from Abraham's era until the Resurrection, and mankind as a whole, into two parts. In the first part of time, God sent prophets in whom were many virtues, and they came one after another and also together in a single era, all of them from the heirs of Isaac (peace be upon him). Then in the second part of time, He brought forth from the descendants of his other son, Ishmael, one who combined all that was among them, and sent him to all creation. He is Muhammad (ﷺ), and He made him the Seal of the Prophets. The creation remained upon the religion of the descendants of Isaac for more than four thousand years, so it is not unlikely that creation will remain upon the religion of the descendants of Ishmael for a similar period.

[Page 51]

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 28–30:**

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed, you commit an abomination that no one among the worlds has committed before you."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the road, and commit the evil in your gathering?" But the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of God, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, support me against the corrupt people."﴾

The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "Lut" is as we mentioned in His words ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾, and the exegesis is as we mentioned there. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: Abraham said to his people ﴿Worship God﴾, while about Lot here it is said that he said to his people ﴿You approach the abomination﴾. We say: when God mentioned Lot alongside Abraham, and Lot was in the time of Abraham, He did not mention about Lot that he commanded his people to monotheism, although a messenger must say that. We say: the account of Lot and others here was mentioned by God in summary, so He confined Himself to what was specific to Lot, which is the prohibition of the abomination, and did not mention his command to monotheism, even though he said it in another place, where He said ﴿Worship God; you have no god other than Him﴾. This is because Abraham had already brought that and preceded him, so it became as if it were specific to him, and Lot was conveying that from Abraham.

As for the prohibition of the deed of the people of Lot, it was specific to Lot, because Abraham did not manifest that in his time and did not forbid them from it. So He mentioned each one with what was specific to him and what preceded others with it.

The second issue: Why did He call that act an abomination (fahisha)? We say: the fahisha is the ugly thing whose ugliness is apparent. Furthermore, desire and anger are two qualities of ugliness, were it not for a benefit for which God would not have created them in man. The benefit of carnal desire is the preservation of the species through the procreation of the individual. This benefit is not achieved except by the existence of the child and its survival after the father. For if it existed and died before the father, the species would perish with the perishing of the first generation. But fornication is the fulfilment of desire and does not lead to the survival of the species, because we have explained that the building up is by existence and the survival of the child after the father. Fornication, although it leads to the existence of the child, does not lead to its survival, because when the waters become mixed, the father does not know his child, so he does not take care of its upbringing and its maintenance, and it is lost and perishes, and so the benefit of survival is not attained. Thus fornication is a vile desire empty of the benefit for which it was created; it is an ugly thing whose ugliness is apparent, since no benefit covers it, and so it is an abomination. And if fornication is an abomination even though it leads to the existence of the child, though not to its survival, then sodomy, which does not lead to its existence, is more deserving of being an abomination.

The third issue: The verse indicates the obligation of the prescribed punishment (hadd) for sodomy, because it shares with fornication the quality of being an abomination, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an abomination﴾ (al-Isra: 32). Their sharing in the abomination suits restraint from it, so whatever was legislated as a deterrent there is legislated as a deterrent here. Although this is an analogy (qiyas, analogical reasoning), its common cause (jami') is derived from the verse. Another aspect is that God made the punishment of those who commit it the raining down of stones, since He rained stones upon them immediately. So whoever commits it must be punished by the raining of stones upon him immediately, which is stoning (rajm).

His words ﴿no one has preceded you in it﴾ may bear two meanings:

One: that no one before them had committed this ugly act, and this is apparent.

The second: that before them perhaps someone had committed it, rarely, but they exaggerated in it, so He said to them, "No one has preceded you in it," as one says, "So-and-so has surpassed the stingy in stinginess, and surpassed the base in baseness," when he exceeds them.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the road"﴾ as a clarification of what we mentioned, meaning: you satisfy desire with men while cutting off the customary path with women, which contains the benefit that is the preservation of the species. This shows that it is an ugly thing whose ugliness is not covered by any benefit. At that point this becomes like His words, exalted is He: ﴿"Do you indeed approach men with desire, instead of women?"﴾ (al-A'raf: 81). That is, approaching women is an ugly desire, but covered by a benefit, so for you there is a lawful means of meeting your need in which there is no abomination, and you abandon it and approach men with desire, together with the abomination.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 28–30:**

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Indeed, you commit an abomination that no one among the worlds has committed before you."﴾ ﴿"Do you really approach men, and cut off the road, and commit the evil in your gathering?" The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "Lut" is as we mentioned in His words ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾, and the exegesis is as we mentioned there. Here there are several issues.

We say: when God mentioned Lot alongside Abraham, and Lot was in the time of Abraham, He did not mention about Lot that he commanded his people to monotheism, although a messenger must say that. Furthermore, desire and anger are two qualities of ugliness, were it not for a benefit for which God would not have created them in man. The benefit of carnal desire is the preservation of the species through the procreation of the individual. This benefit is not achieved except by the existence of the child and its survival after the father. For if it existed and died before the father, the species would perish with the perishing of the first generation. But fornication is the fulfilment of desire and does not lead to the survival of the species, because we have explained that the building up is by existence and the survival of the child after the father. Fornication, although it leads to the existence of the child, does not lead to its survival, because when the waters become mixed, the father does not know his child, so he does not take care of its upbringing and its maintenance, and it is lost and perishes, and so the benefit of survival is not attained. Thus fornication is a vile desire empty of the benefit for which it was created; it is an ugly thing whose ugliness is apparent, since no benefit covers it, and so it is an abomination. ﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good news, they said, "We are going to destroy the people of this town; indeed, its people have been wrongdoers." He said, "Indeed, Lut is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾

When Lut prayed against his people, saying, ﴿My Lord, support me﴾, Allah answered his prayer. He commanded His angels to destroy them and sent them as bearers of good news and as warners. They came to Ibrahim (Abraham), gave him the good news of righteous offspring, and said, ﴿Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, meaning the people of Sadum (Sodom). In this verse there are two subtleties.

The first: Allah made them bearers of good news and warners. But good news is an effect of mercy, and warning of destruction is an effect of wrath, and His mercy precedes His wrath. So He placed the good news before the warning. He said, ﴿came to Ibrahim with the good news﴾, then said, ﴿we are going to destroy﴾.

The second: when they mentioned the good news, they did not give a reason, but they said, "We give you good news because you are a messenger," or "because you are a believer," or "because you are just." When they mentioned the destruction, they gave a reason and said, ﴿indeed, its people have been wrongdoers﴾. This is because one who is possessed of bounty does not give his bounty in exchange for anything, while a just one does not punish except for a crime. On this there are two questions.

The first: If someone asks, "What is the connection between this good news and this warning?" We say: when Allah intended to destroy a people, and this would empty the land of its inhabitants, He first informed Ibrahim that He would fill the earth with righteous servants, so that he would not grieve over the destruction of a people from among his own kind.

The second: Concerning the people of Nuh, He said, ﴿So the flood seized them﴾, and I have already said that this indicates they were in their wrongdoing when it seized them, and He did not say, "So it seized them while they were wrongdoers." Here, however, He said, ﴿indeed, its people have been wrongdoers﴾, and did not say, "and indeed they are wrongdoers." We say: there is no difference between the two places regarding their being destroyed while they were persisting in wrongdoing. So He said "it seized them" while they were, at the moment of falling into the punishment, wrongdoers. Here, however, the report is from the angels and concerns the future, where they said, ﴿we are going to destroy﴾. So they said, "We are going to destroy them because Allah has commanded us, and at the time He commanded us, they were wrongdoers." Thus Allah's command is good in the eyes of everyone.
