Here is a subtle point: God's sign of His power exists in both deliverance and destruction, so He mentioned a sign from each category. He placed the signs of deliverance first, because they are the effect of mercy, and He placed the signs of destruction later, because they are the effect of wrath, and His mercy precedes.

The second issue: He said of the ship: ﴿and We made it a sign﴾ and did not say "clear", whereas here He said: "a clear sign." We say: because deliverance by the ship is a matter that every intellect can comprehend, and it may occur to an ignorant person's imagination that deliverance by the ship does not require anything else. But the sign here is the sinking and the turning upside down of inhabited dwellings, which is not customary, and is only by the will of a Powerful One who singles it out for one place rather than another and one time rather than another. So it is clear, and no ignorant person can say: "This is a matter that happens in this way." He could have said of the ship: "Deliverance by it is a matter that happens in this way," until it was said to him: "From where did he know that they needed it? And if the water had lasted until their provisions ran out, how would they have been delivered? And if God had sent a violent wind upon them, what would their condition have been?"

The third issue: He said there: ﴿for the worlds﴾, and here He said: ﴿for a people who reason﴾. We say: because the ship exists in all regions of the world, so every people has a likeness of Noah's ship by which they remember his condition, and when they board it they seek deliverance from God, and no one trusts merely in the ship; rather, he is always trembling of heart, humbling himself before God, the Exalted, seeking deliverance. As for the trace of destruction in Lot's lands, it is in a specific place that no one knows of except those who pass by it, reach it, and have an intellect that knows that this is from God, the One who wills, because of His singling out one place over another and its existence in one time after another time.

[Page 57]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah, and hope for the Last Day, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief."﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes.﴾

When He had completed the second narrative in a concise manner for the sake of its lesson, He moved on to the third and said: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother.﴾ The exegetes differed concerning Madyan. Some said it is originally the name of a man, from whom descendants came, and it became known as a tribe, like Tamim and Qays and others. Others said it is the name of a water source to which the people are attributed, and it became known as the name of the people. The first view seems more correct, because Allah attributed the water to Madyan when He said: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ (al-Qasas: 23). If it were the name of the water, the attribution would be invalid or not literal, and the principle in an attribution (idafa) is literal distinction. As for His saying ﴿their brother﴾, it is said that this is because Shu'ayb was of their lineage. In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Allah said regarding Nuh: ﴿And We certainly sent Nuh to his people﴾ (Hud: 25). Here He mentioned Nuh first and defined the people by attributing them to him. The same applies to Ibrahim and Lut. Here He mentioned the people first and then attached to them "their brother Shu'ayb." We say: the principle in all instances is that the people are mentioned first and then their messenger, because the one who sends does not dispatch a messenger to an unspecified group. Rather, a people or a person arises who needs information from the Sender, so He sends to them whomever He chooses. However, the people of Nuh, Ibrahim, and Lut had no specific name or particular lineage by which they were known, so they were identified by their prophet, and it was said: "the people of Nuh" and "the people of Lut." As for the people of Shu'ayb, Hud, and Salih, they had a known lineage by which they were famous among people, so the speech followed its original form, and Allah said: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ and said: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ (al-A'raf: 65).

**The second issue:** Why is it not mentioned about Lut that he commanded his people to worship and affirm Allah's oneness (tawhid), while it is mentioned about Shu'ayb? We say: we have mentioned that Lut had a people, and he was from the people of Ibrahim and in his time. Ibrahim had preceded him in this and strove for it until the matter of tawhid became well known among the creation through Ibrahim. So it is not mentioned about Lut, but only what was specific to him, namely the prohibition against immorality (fahisha) and other things, though he too would command tawhid, since there is no messenger whose speech is not mostly about tawhid. As for Shu'ayb, he came after the extinction of that people, so he was himself the origin for tawhid as well, and so he began with it and said: ﴿Worship Allah﴾.

**The third issue:** Faith (iman) is not complete except with tawhid, and a command to worship does not by itself convey it, because whoever worships Allah and also worships another is a polytheist. How then did He suffice with His saying ﴿Worship Allah﴾? We say: this command conveys tawhid, because whoever sees another serving Zayd and 'Amr there, and that one is greater or is the master of Zayd, when told "Serve 'Amr," he understands from it that he is commanded to direct the service to him. Likewise, if someone has a single dinar and wants to give it to Zayd, and he is told "Give it to 'Amr," he understands from it: do not give it to Zayd. So we say: they were occupied with worshipping other than Allah, and Allah is the owner of that other. So Shu'ayb said to them: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, and they understood from it the abandonment of worshipping others. Or we say: each person has one soul, and he wants to place it in the worship of other than Allah, so Shu'ayb said to them: place it in its proper place, which is the worship of Allah, and tawhid was understood from it. Then He said: ﴿and hope for the Last Day﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is "do what will make you hope for the outcome," since a speaker may say to another "be sensible," and its meaning is "act in the manner of one who is sensible." His saying ﴿and hope for the Last Day﴾ contains several issues:

**The first issue:** This indicates the soundness of our school of thought (madhhabuna). For according to us, whoever worships Allah throughout his life, Allah rewards him out of bounty (tafaddul), and it is not obligatory upon Him to do so, because the worshipper has already received blessings such that, even if he were to add to what he has done, he would not have fulfilled the duty of gratitude. And whoever thanks the Benefactor for blessings that preceded, the Benefactor is not obliged to increase them; and if He increases them, that is a kindness from Him to him and a favour upon him. So we say: His saying ﴿and hope for [the Day]﴾ after His saying ﴿Worship Allah﴾ indicates bounty and not obligation, for bounty is hoped for, whereas what is owed by the Just One is something one is certain of.

**The second issue:** He said ﴿and hope for the Last Day﴾ and did not say "and fear Him," even though that Day is frightening to all, and for many people it is not something to be hoped for because of their wickedness, their immorality, and their love of this world; only a few of His servants hope for it. We say: when He mentioned tawhid by way of affirmation, saying ﴿Worship﴾, and did not mention it by way of negation, nor said "and do not worship other than Him," He used the wording of hope, because worshipping Allah is hoped to bring good in both abodes. There is another aspect too: Allah related in the narrative of Ibrahim that he said: ﴿You have taken idols only as a bond of affection between you in the life of this world; but on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 25). Here He said: do not be like those mentioned earlier who did not hope for the Last Day, and so they limited themselves to affection in the life of this world. Rather, hope for the Last Day and act for it.

Then He said: ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief.﴾ It is possible to say that ﴿causing mischief﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), as one says "stand up standing," meaning "standing." And His saying ﴿do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾ is like the speaker's saying "sit sitting," because 'ayth (corruption) and fasad (mischief) have the same meaning. He gathered the commands and prohibitions in His saying ﴿Worship Allah﴾ and His saying ﴿do not commit corruption﴾.

Then his people denied him after he had delivered and made clear [the message]. Allah related this about them by His saying: ﴿But they denied him, so the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** What is reported of Shu'ayb is commands and prohibitions, and a command is not subject to being affirmed or denied as true or false, for whoever says to another "Stand up" cannot be told "You are lying." We say: Shu'ayb was saying: "Allah is one, so worship Him; the gathering (hashr) is certain, so hope for it; corruption is forbidden, so do not approach it." These matters contain informative statements, and they denied him in what he informed them of.

**The second issue:** He said here and in al-A'raf: ﴿so the earthquake seized them﴾, and in Hud He said: ﴿so the earthquake seized them﴾ [as well]. The narrative is one. We say there is no contradiction between them, for the Cry (al-sayha) was a cause of the quake, either the quake of the earth, since it is said that Jibril cried out and the earth shook from his cry, or the quaking of hearts, for their hearts trembled from it. Attributing an event to its cause does not conflict with attributing it to the cause of its cause, since it is valid to say "he drank water and became strong" and "he drank and became strong" in one and the same instance.

**The third issue:** Where He said ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾ He said ﴿in their abodes (diyar)﴾, and where He said ﴿so the earthquake seized them﴾ He said ﴿in their home (dar)﴾. We say: the intended meaning of "home" is "abodes," and the attribution to a plural may be in the plural form, or in the singular form when there is no ambiguity. The wording differed for a subtle reason: the quake is awesome in itself, so it did not need an intensifier. As for the Cry, it is not awesome in itself, but since that Cry was so great that it caused an earthquake in the earth, He mentioned the abodes in the plural, so that its awesomeness might be known. The quake, in the sense of an earthquake, is great for everyone, so it did not need something to emphasize its importance. It was also said that the Cry was more general, since it encompassed the earth and the atmosphere, whereas the earthquake was only in the earth, so He mentioned the abodes there.

However, this is weak, because the "home" and the "abodes" are the place of prostration, not the place of the Cry or the quake, for they did not become prostrate except in their homes.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So each one We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a violent wind, and among them were those seized by the Cry, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah was not one to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Allah mentioned four things: the punishment by the hasib (a violent wind carrying stones). It was said that it was by heated stones that fall upon one of them and pass through to the other side, and in this there is an allusion to fire. The punishment by the Cry (al-sayha) is a surging air, for the sound is said to be caused by the surging of the air and its reaching the membrane over the opening of the ear, which is the eardrum (al-simakh), so it strikes it and it is perceived. The punishment by the earth swallowing (al-khasf) is being submerged in the dust, and the punishment by drowning (al-ighraq) is by water. Thus the punishment came through the four elements, and the human being is composed of them, and by them his constitution stands, and by their cause his survival and continuance endure. So when Allah wills the destruction of a human being, He makes that from which his existence came a cause of his non-existence, and that by which his survival is maintained a cause of his perishing.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah was not one to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ That is, He did not wrong them by destroying them; rather, they wronged themselves by associating partners with Allah. There is another, subtler interpretation: that Allah did not wrong them, meaning He did not place them in other than their proper place, for their proper place is honour, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam﴾ (al-Isra, 17:70). But they wronged themselves in that they placed themselves, despite their nobility, in the worship of an idol, despite its baseness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 41:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The likeness of those who take protectors other than God is like the spider that takes a house﴾

When God, exalted is He, had made clear that He destroyed those who associated partners with Him in this world, and punished those who denied Him in the next, and that the deity they had taken did not benefit them in either abode, nor did their bowing and prostration avert that from them, He gave the likeness of their taking that deity as worshipped to the spider's taking a house, which neither protects one who seeks shelter nor gives rest to one who dwells in it. In this verse there are subtleties which we shall mention in several issues:

The first issue: What is the wisdom in choosing this likeness from among all the other likenesses? We say that there are several aspects to it:

The first: A house ought to have certain features: a dividing wall, a roofing that gives shade, a door that can be closed, and matters by which one benefits and finds comfort. If it does not have these, then it must have one of two things.

Either a dividing wall that keeps off the cold, or a shading roof that repels the heat from it. If neither of these is present, it is like the open desert and is not a house. But the spider's house neither shelters from the cold nor covers from the heat. Likewise, the one worshipped ought to have creation and provision, and bring benefits and repel harms by it. If these matters are not all gathered, then at the least there must be the repelling of harm or the bringing of benefit. For whoever is not like this is, in relation to him, equal to the nonexistent. Thus, just as the spider gains nothing of the meanings of a house by taking that dwelling, so the disbeliever gains nothing of the meanings of protectors by taking idols as protectors.

The second: The least level of a house is that it should provide shade. For a house of stone gives shade and also repels wind, water, fire and dust; a house of wood gives shade and repels heat and cold, but does not repel strong wind, water or fire; and the tent, which is a dwelling of hair, or the pavilion made of cloth, if it repels nothing else, at least gives shade and repels the heat of the sun. But the spider's house gives no shade, for the sun with its rays passes through it. Likewise, the highest level of the worshipped one is that his command is executed over others; if not, then that his command is executed over the worshipper; and if not, then at least that the worshipper's command is not executed over him. But their worshipped deity is under their subjugation: if they wish, they exalt it, and if they wish, they debase it.

The third: The lowest level of a house is that if it is not a cause of stability and comfort, it does not become a cause of dispersal and separation. But the spider's house becomes a cause of the spider's disturbance, for if the spider remained for a period in a corner without intending or leaving it, then when it weaves upon itself and takes a house, the owner follows it, cleaning the house of it and wiping it with rough, harmful cloths that hurt the spider's body. Likewise, the worshipper, by reason of worship, ought to deserve reward, and if he does not deserve it, then at the least he should not deserve punishment because of it. Yet the disbeliever, by reason of worship, deserves punishment.

Page 61
The second issue: God likened their taking idols as protectors to the spider's weaving its web into a house, and He did not liken it to the web itself. This is for two reasons:

One of them: Its weaving has a benefit for it which would not have been achieved without it, namely catching flies with it, without losing by it anything greater. Their taking idols, although it gives them only what is less than a fly in worldly goods, yet loses them what is greater than these, namely the Last Abode which is better and more lasting. So their taking is not like the spider's weaving.

The second aspect: its weaving is beneficial, but its taking that web as a house is a vain matter. Likewise, if they had taken the idols as signs of the existence of God and of the attributes of His perfection, and as proofs of the qualities of His honour and the descriptions of His majesty, that would have been wisdom. But they took them as protectors, like the spider's making the web a house, and both are vain.

The third issue: Just as this likeness was correct at the beginning, so it is correct at the end. For when a wind blows upon the spider's house, no trace or sign of it is seen; rather it becomes scattered dust. Likewise their deeds for the idols, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will turn to what they have done of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ (al-Furqan: 23).

The fourth issue: He said: ﴿The likeness of those who take protectors other than God﴾ and did not say "gods," as a指 reference to the nullification of hidden associationism as well, for whoever worships God for the sake of showing off to others has taken another as a protector, so his likeness is the likeness of the spider which takes its web as a house.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, the weakest of houses is the house of the spider, if they only knew.﴾

This is an indication of what we have explained, that every house has either the benefit of providing shade or something else, and the spider's house is too weak to provide that benefit, because it is destroyed by the slightest thing, and no trace or remnant of it remains. Likewise is their deed, ﴿if they only knew.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what they invoke besides Him of anything. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an added emphasis on the parable, since they invoke besides Him nothing at all, meaning: what they invoke is not anything. And He is Mighty and Wise, so how is it permissible for a rational person to abandon the All-Powerful, the Wise, and occupy himself with worshipping that which is not a thing at all? From this it is understood that he made *mā* a negation, which is correct. Knowledge relates to the whole statement, as when a speaker says: "I know that Allah is One, that is true," meaning: I know this proposition. If, however, we take *mā* as relative (*khabariyya*), the meaning becomes: "what they invoke of anything, Allah knows it, and He is the Mighty, the Wise, able to annihilate it and destroy them, but He is Wise and gives them respite so that destruction comes after clear proof and life comes after clear proof." From here the address is with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). On this view, if someone asks: what is the connection of this verse to the preceding parable? We say: when He said, "Their likeness is that of the spider," it was possible for the disbeliever to say, "I do not worship these idols which I take, and which are under my control; rather, they are the image of a star under whose control I am, and from it comes my benefit, my harm, my good and my evil, my existence and my continuance, so to it I prostrate and to it I give honor." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: Allah knows that all that they worship besides Allah is like the spider's house, because the star, the angel, and everything other than Allah neither benefits nor harms except by Allah's permission. So your worship of the absent is like your worship of the present, and there is no deity except Allah, and there is no god besides Him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And these parables We set forth for the people.﴾

The disbelievers said: How can the Creator of the earth and the heavens strike parables with insects and creeping things, such as the gnat, the fly, and the spider? It is said in reply: parables are struck for people so that, if you are not like cattle, there may arise in you through them an awareness of what compels your aversion to what you are engaged in. This is because comparison affects the soul with an effect like that of proof. Thus when the wise person says to one who backbites, "You, through backbiting, are as if you were eating the flesh of a dead man, because you have fallen upon this man while he is absent, unable to understand what you say or to hear it so as to respond, like one who falls upon a corpse and eats from it while he does not know what is being done to him and cannot repel it, and if he did know, his nature would recoil from it, just as it recoils when told that it brings punishment and inherits retribution."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verses 43–44:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And none understand them except the knowledgeable.﴾

That is, its reality. That the matter is as it is, none knows except the one in whom knowledge of the falsehood of everything other than God, and the corruption of worshipping anything besides Him, has been established. There is also a judgmental meaning in this: intuitive knowledge (*al-ʿilm al-ḥadsī*, knowledge grasped by immediate intuition) is known by the person of intellect (*al-ʿāqil*), while subtle knowledge acquired through reasoning (*al-ʿilm al-fikrī al-daqīq*) is understood by the one who has knowledge (*al-ʿālim*). This is because when a clear matter is presented to the person of intellect, he perceives it as it truly is, since the object of perception is evident and he is a person of intellect, and he does not need to have knowledge of other things beforehand. As for what is subtle, it requires prior knowledge, so there must be a knowledgeable person. Furthermore, something may be extremely subtle, so that one perceives it without perceiving it in its entirety, and one understands it when one is a knowledgeable person. Given this, His saying ﴿And none understand them except the knowledgeable﴾ means: He has struck examples for people, and their reality and all the benefits in them are not grasped except by the scholars.

Then, when the Exalted commanded creation to believe and made the truth manifest through proof, and the unbelievers did not do what He commanded them, and He related to them stories containing lessons, and warned them of destruction of those who passed away for their disbelief, and clarified the weakness of their argument through the parable, and they were not guided by this to the right path, and people despaired of them, He consoled the believers with His saying:

﴿God created the heavens and the earth in truth. Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

That is: if they do not believe, their disbelief does not produce doubt about the soundness of your religion, nor does their doubt affect the strength of your certainty. For God's creation of the heavens and the earth in truth is a manifest clarification and a dazzling proof for the believers, even if no unbeliever on the face of the earth believes in it. In the verse there is an issue by which the explanation of the verse becomes clear, namely: how did God restrict the sign in the creation of the heavens and the earth to the believers, when in their creation there is a sign for every person of intellect, as God said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾ (Luqman: 25), and God said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾ up to His saying ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾ (al-Baqarah: 164). We say: the creation of the heavens and the earth is a sign for every person of intellect, and their creation in truth is a sign only for the believers. Its explanation, in terms of transmission (*al-naql*) and reason (*al-ʿaql*), is as follows. As for transmission, it is His saying: ﴿We did not create them except in truth, but most of them do not know﴾ (al-Dukhan: 39), which excluded most people from knowledge that their creation was in truth, although He affirmed that all know that He created them, when He said: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾. As for reason, it is that the person of intellect, when he first looks at the creation of the heavens and the earth, knows that they have a creator, who is God. Then, whoever God guides does not cut off his contemplation of them upon mere recognition of this, but says that He created them firmly and skillfully, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿in truth﴾, because what is not made with skill decays and perishes and thus becomes false. When he knows that He created them skillfully, he says that He is Powerful and Perfect, since He created, and Knowing, whose knowledge is comprehensive, since He perfected [them]. So he says that there is nothing hidden from His knowledge, neither the parts of the existents on earth nor in the heavens, and He is not unable to gather them, just as He gathered the parts of beings and originated things. Thus he affirms the resurrection of those in the graves and the sending of the Messenger, and he knows the oneness of God, for if there were more than one god, both would have been corrupted and would have perished, and they both exist in truth. Thus faith is fully established in him, from the creation of what He created in its excellent order.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 45 (part 1 of 2):

Then, when God, exalted is He, consoled the believers with this verse, He consoled His Messenger with His words: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish the prayer. Indeed, the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing.﴾

That is, if you grieve over their disbelief, then recite what has been revealed to you, so that you know that Noah, Lot and others were in the same situation as you. They conveyed the message and exerted themselves in presenting the proof, but they did not rescue their peoples from error and ignorance. For this reason He said, ﴿Recite﴾ and did not say "against them," because the recitation, after despair of them, was only for consoling the heart of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: When a Messenger has a book, and reads it once and it is not heeded, there is no benefit in reading it for himself. We say that the Book revealed with the Prophet who was sent is not like this. The books carried by the Messengers are of two kinds. One kind contains greetings and speech, which is fully achieved by reading it once. The other kind contains a universal law that the subjects need at all times, like when a king writes a letter saying: "We have lifted from you such-and-such innovation, established among you such-and-such sunnah, and sent you this letter, which contains all of that." Such a letter should be like a pattern that each governor after another weaves upon. Such a book is not read and then left aside; rather it is hung up in a high place, and often its copy is inscribed on a board and fixed above the prayer niches (mihrabs) so that it is always before the eyes. Likewise, the Book of God with His Messenger Muhammad is a universal law containing healing for all the worlds. Therefore it is obligatory to recite it again and again, so that it reaches the level of tawatur (mass transmission), is transmitted from generation to generation, is taken by one people from another, and remains fixed in the hearts through the passing of ages.

The second aspect: Books are of three kinds. There is a book whose reading is disliked only for others, such as stories: whoever reads a narrative once does not read it again except for someone else, and then when that other person hears it, he does not read it except for yet another who has not heard it; if he read it to them repeatedly, they would become bored. There is a book that is not repeated except for oneself, such as grammar, jurisprudence and the like. And there is a book that is recited again and again, both for oneself and for others, such as good admonitions. These are repeated for others, and whenever one hears them, one delights in them, one's heart softens to them, one seeks to hear them again, and whenever they enter the hearing, the whisperings leave with the tears. They are also repeated for the speaker himself, for the speaker often delights in a good word, and each time he repeats it, it becomes more pleasant, sweeter and more firmly fixed in the heart and more penetrating, until he almost weeps blood from its tenderness, even if weeping causes him blindness. Given this, the Qur'an belongs to the third kind, and in addition it contains stories, jurisprudence and grammar. So its recitation at every time has a benefit.

Page 64

The second issue: Why did God specify these two things for the command, the recitation of the Book and the establishment of the prayer? We say, for two reasons.

The first: When God wished to console the heart of Muhammad, peace be upon him, He said to him: The Messenger is an intermediary between two ends, from God to creation. If one end does not connect with him and they do not accept him, the other end remains connected. Do you not see that when a messenger's message is not accepted, he turns toward the one who sent him? So when you recite your Book and they do not accept you, turn your face toward Me and establish the prayer for My sake.

The second reason: The acts of worship specific to the servant are three. One is the true belief (i'tiqad), one is verbal, which is the good remembrance (dhikr), and one is bodily and external, which is righteous action. But belief is not repeated, for whoever believes something cannot believe it again once more; rather it continues steadily. The Prophet, peace be upon him, possessed this by direct witnessing ('iyan), more perfectly than what is acquired by demonstration (bayan). So he was not commanded with it, because it cannot be repeated. But remembrance can be repeated, and bodily worship is likewise. So He commanded him with these two, saying: Recite the Book and establish the prayer.

* * *

The third issue: How does the prayer forbid indecency and wrongdoing? We say: Some exegetes said that what is meant by the prayer is the Qur'an, and it forbids them, that is, it contains a prohibition of them. This is far-fetched, because taking the Qur'an to be meant by "the prayer" in this context, after His saying before it, ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you﴾, is far from the correct understanding. Others said that it means the prayer itself, and that it forbids them as long as the servant is in the prayer, because he cannot occupy himself with either of them. We say: this is so, but this is not what is meant, for otherwise it would not be a complete praise of the prayer, since other activities are often like this, such as sleep at its time and other things. So we say: what is meant is that the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing absolutely. On this basis some exegetes said: the prayer is the one performed with presence of heart (hudur), and it forbids them. It has been transmitted from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain from sins, it only increases him in distance (from God)." We say: the prayer that is valid according to the Law forbids both matters absolutely, and it is the one performed by the responsible person for God. Even if he intends by it showing off (riya'), his prayer is not valid according to the Law and he is obligated to repeat it. This is evident, for whoever intends by his ablution the prayer and cooling himself down, it is said it is not valid. How much more so whoever intends by his prayer God and other than Him. Having established this, we say: the prayer forbids in several respects.

The first: Whoever serves a king of great station, abundant in benevolence, who holds him in high rank, and sees a servant of his whom the king has driven away with a rejection that cannot be imagined to be reversed, and who has lost the good so that its attainment is no longer hoped for, it is customarily inconceivable that such a favored person should abandon the king's service and enter into obedience to that rejected one. Likewise, when a servant prays to God, he becomes a servant of Him and attains the station of one who prays, communing with his Lord. It is inconceivable for him to abandon the worship of God and enter under the obedience of the accursed Satan. But the perpetrator of indecency and wrongdoing is under the obedience of Satan. Therefore the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing.

The second: Whoever deals with filth, such as the garbage collector and the street sweeper, has clean clothing which, when he wears it, he does not handle filth with. The higher his garment, the more he, while wearing it, refrains from filth. If one of them wears a gilded silk brocade, it is customarily inconceivable that he handle those things. Likewise, when the servant prays, he dons the garment of piety, because he stands before God, placing his right hand upon his left, in the posture of one who stands in the sight of a dignified king. The garment of piety is the best garment, whose relation to the heart is higher than the relation of gilded brocade to the body. So whoever wears this garment, it is inconceivable for him to handle the filth of indecency and wrongdoing. Moreover, the prayers recur one after another, so this garment continues, and so the abstention continues.

The third: Whoever is master of himself sits wherever he wishes. But when he enters the service of a king and is given a post that has a specific station, the holder of that post sits only in that place. If he wanted to sit among the shoe-racks, he would not be permitted. Likewise, when the servant prays, he enters the obedience of God and no longer remains under his own authority, and he attains a specific station, for he has become one of the companions of the right hand. If he wanted to stand in a place other than his own, which is the station of the companions of the left, he would not be permitted. But the perpetrator of

Page 65

indecency and wrongdoing is among the companions of the left. This aspect is an indication of God's protection (ismah), meaning: whoever prays, God protects him from indecency and wrongdoing.

The fourth, which agrees with what the reports have related: Whoever is far from the king, like the commoner, the crier and the one who makes his living in the marketplace, does not care what actions he commits. He eats in the shop of the cheap-food sellers and the tripe-sellers, and sits with the rabble of people. But when he gains a slight nearness to the king, such as when he becomes one of the palace guards, the commanders or the stewards at the king's court, that nearness does not prevent him from engaging in what he used to do. But when his nearness increases and his rank rises until he becomes an amir, then this rank prevents him from eating in that place and sitting with those former companions. Likewise, when the servant prays and prostrates, he attains some nearness, according to God's saying: ﴿And prostrate and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19]. When that measure of nearness prevents him from sins and prohibited acts, then by repeating the prayer and prostration his station increases, until he sees on himself the traces of honour, such that he finds even minor faults repugnant to himself, let alone major sins.

There is another rational interpretation of the verse, which is confirmed by what has been transmitted: that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ is that it forbids ta'til (denial of God's attributes or existence) and shirk (association). Ta'til is the denial of God's existence, and shirk is the affirmation of divinity for other than God.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 29, verse 45 (part 2 of 2):

We say: *ta'til* (the denial of the Creator, or of His attributes) is a foul belief, because *al-fahsha'* is that which is ugly and manifestly ugly. But the existence of God is more evident than the sun, and there is nothing except that it contains a manifest sign pointing to God. The denial of what is manifest is itself manifestly a denial. So the saying that there is no god is ugly, and *shirk* (associating partners with God) is *munkar* (objectionable). This is because God, exalted, when He called objectionable the one who attributes a son to other than the father, although it is possible for Him to have a son, said: ﴿Their mothers are none but those who gave birth to them, and indeed they say an objectionable word and a falsehood﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2]. So the polytheist who says "the angels are the daughters of God," and attributes offspring to the One who has not begotten and who cannot have offspring, how could his saying not be objectionable? Therefore the *salah* (ritual prayer) forbids this *fahsha'* and this *munkar*.

This is because the servant, when he first begins the prayer, says "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). By his saying "Allah" he negates *ta'til*, and by his saying "akbar" he negates *tashrik* (the ascribing of partners), because a partner is not greater than the other partner in that in which they share. Then, when he says "bismillah" (in the name of God), he negates *ta'til*, and when he says "al-Rahman al-Rahim" he negates *shirk*, because al-Rahman is the One who gives existence by creating through mercy, and al-Rahim is the One who gives continuance by providing sustenance through mercy. Then when he says "al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin" (all praise is for God, Lord of the worlds), he affirms by his saying "al-hamdu lillah" the opposite of *ta'til*, and by his saying "Lord of the worlds" the opposite of *shirk*. Then when he says "iyyaka na'budu" (You alone we worship), by placing "iyyaka" first he negates both *ta'til* and *shirk*. Likewise by his saying "wa-iyyaka nasta'in" (and You alone we ask for help). Then when he says "ihdina al-sirat" (guide us to the path) he negates *ta'til*, because the seeker of the path has an aim, whereas the one who denies has no aim. And by his saying "al-mustaqim" (the straight) he negates *shirk*, because *al-mustaqim* is the nearest, and the polytheist worships idols, until he worships a likeness which the Lord of the worlds did not make, and they think that these will intercede for them, whereas the worship of God without an intermediary is nearer. On this basis, up to the end of the prayer, he says in it: "ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah" (I bear witness that there is no god but God), and thereby negates both *shirk* and *ta'til*.

Here there is a subtle point: the beginning of the prayer is the word "Allah," and its end is the word "Allah" in his saying "ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah," so that the worshipper knows that from the beginning of the prayer to its end he is with God. If someone says: there remains in the prayer his saying "wa-ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah" (and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God), and the blessing upon the Messenger and the salutation, we say: these matters entered at its end for a meaning external to the essence of the prayer. This is because the prayer is purely the remembrance of God and nothing else. But when the servant, through the prayer, reaches God and attains to union with God, it does not occur to his heart that he has become self-sufficient, independent, and free of need of the Messenger. This is like one who draws near to the sultan, who is then deceived by that and does not turn to the deputies and chamberlains. So it is said to him: you are in this lofty station by the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ), and you are not free of need of him. So say, along with my remembrance: "Muhammad is the Messenger of God." Then, when you know that all of this is by the blessing of his guidance, mention his favour by blessing him. Then, when you return from your ascent and reach your brothers, greet them with peace and convey my greetings to them, as is the order of travellers. And know that the form of the prayer is a form that contains awe, for its beginning is standing before God as a slave stands before a sultan, and then its end is kneeling before God as one kneels before a sultan, to whom he has granted the honour of being seated. It is as if the servant, when he stood and praised God, was honoured by God and was made to sit, so he knelt. In this kneeling there is a subtle point: whoever knelt in this world before his Lord in this manner will not have a kneeling in the Hereafter, and he will not be among those about whom God said: ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein kneeling﴾ [Maryam: 72].

* *
* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greatest, and God knows what you do﴾.

When He mentioned two matters, namely the recitation of the Book and the establishment of the prayer, He explained what necessitates that their performance be in the most eloquent manner of glorification. So He said: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greatest﴾. You, when you mention your fathers with the good qualities that they possess, rejoice at that and mention them with the fullness of your mouths and hearts. But the remembrance of God is greatest, so it is fitting that it be in the most eloquent manner of glorification. As for the prayer, it is likewise, because God knows what you do, and this is the best of your deeds, so it is fitting that it be done in the manner of glorification. In His saying ﴿And the remembrance of God is greatest﴾, with the omission of specifying that than which it is greater, there is a subtle point: God did not say "greater than the remembrance of so-and-so," because whatever is described as great in relation to another has a relation to it. Hence one does not say "the mountain is greater than a mustard seed," but one says "this mountain is greater than that mountain." So the thing compared was dropped, as if He said: the remembrance of God has greatness for Him, not for anything else. This is like what is said in the prayer: "Allahu akbar," meaning greatness belongs to Him and not to another.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best, except for those of them who have wronged. And say, "We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you. Our God and your God is one, and we are Muslims [in submission] to Him."﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you the Book. Those to whom We gave the Scripture believe in it, and among these [people] there are those who believe in it. And none rejects Our signs except the disbelievers.﴾

When Allah explained the method of guiding the polytheists, and those who benefited benefited, and despair arose regarding those who refused, He explained the method of guiding the People of the Scripture (ahl al-kitab). ﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], and so on. As for the People of the Scripture, they came with everything good except acknowledging the Prophet (peace be upon him). They affirmed the oneness [of God], and they believed in the revelation of books, the sending of messengers, and the Resurrection. Therefore, in return for their good, they are argued with first in the best manner: their opinions are not belittled, and their forefathers are not attributed to error, unlike the polytheist. Then, based on this, His saying ﴿except those of them who have wronged﴾ is a clarification of another good aspect, namely that what is meant is: except those of them who associated partners [with Allah] by ascribing a son to Allah and by saying "third of three." For they resembled the polytheists in the reprehensible saying, so they are wrongdoers, because association (shirk) is a great wrong. Therefore they are argued with in a harsher manner, to denounce their statement and to make clear their ignorance. Others said: What is meant by "those to whom We gave the Scripture" are those among the People of the Scripture who preceded Muhammad (ﷺ) in time, and "among these" are those among the People of the Scripture who are in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is closer, because those to whom He gave the Scripture in reality are the Prophets, for Allah did not give the Scripture except to the Prophets, as He said: ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Scripture﴾, and He said: ﴿And We gave David a Psalter﴾ [al-Isra': 55], and He said: ﴿He has given me the Scripture﴾ [Maryam: 30]. When we take the discourse in this sense, it does not admit specification, because all the Prophets believed in all the Prophets. Then God says: ﴿You did not recite any scripture before it, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾. This is another level, after what was mentioned earlier, according to the sequence. That is because the disputant, when he mentions a disputed issue, such as someone saying: "Zakat is obligatory on the property of a minor," and it is said to him, "Why?", he replies: "Just as maintenance is obligatory on his property." He does not first mention the common element between the two. If the seeker is satisfied with the mere comparison and perceives the common element himself, that is well. If he does not perceive it, or is not satisfied, he states the common element, saying: "Both are property that exceeds need, so it is obligatory; likewise here." Here, He first mentioned the comparison with His words: ﴿And thus We revealed to you﴾, then He mentioned the common element, which is the miracle, and said: the knowledge that those scriptures were sent down is only through a miracle, and this Qur'an came from one who neither wrote nor read, so the very miracle makes known that it was sent down. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ contain a subtle meaning, namely that if the Prophet had been a reader and writer, that would not have required that this speech be his speech, for all the scribes and readers on earth would be unable to produce it. But on that supposition the falsifier would have had a basis for doubt, whereas as things stand there is no basis for his doubt, so it is more effective in refuting him. This is like His words: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], that is, like Muhammad (ﷺ). And like His words: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. This is the Book about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1–2].

Page 69

When He finished mentioning a proof from the side of the Prophet (peace be upon him), He mentioned their doubt, which lies in drawing a distinction between the basis of comparison (*al-maqis 'alayh*) and the case being compared (*al-maqis*). They said: "You claim that a Book has been sent down to you just as it was sent down to Musa and Isa. But this is not so, because Musa was given nine signs by which it was known that the Book was from God, and you have not been given any of them." Then God, exalted is He, guided His Prophet to answers to this doubt. Among them is His saying: ﴿Signs are only with God.﴾ Its meaning is that the Prophet (ﷺ) claimed prophethood, and a miraculous sign is not a condition of prophethood. A messenger is first sent and calls to God. Then, if the people hesitate to accept him or ask him for a proof, God, if He is merciful to them, makes His messengership clear, and if He is not merciful to them, He does not make it clear. So He said: "I am now a messenger." As for the sign, God, if He wills, will send it down, and if He does not will it, He will not send it down. This is because what is a necessary attribute (*darurat*) of a thing: when God creates a thing, it must be that He creates it, just as place is a necessary attribute of a human being. So God does not create a human being without creating a place for him, or creating it along with him. But prophethood and a miracle are not like this. When God creates a messenger and makes him a messenger, it is not a necessary attribute of his that a miracle be known for him. This is why the messengership of messengers such as Kashith (Seth), Idris and Shu'ayb is known, yet no miracle is known for them. If it is said that their messengership is known, we say: whoever's messengership is established without a miracle, our Prophet is likewise; he has no need for a miracle, because his messengership has been known through the words of Musa and Isa. Thus the falsity of their saying "Why has no sign been sent down to him?" becomes clear. This is because they demanded that the sign precede him, although it is not a condition that it precede him. Yet if they had a question, its proper form would be for them to say: "O claimant, we neither deny nor accept you, but we want God to make clear to us a sign that will free us from accepting a pretender and rejecting a prophet, and by which we may know that you are a prophet and believe in you." After that, it would not be far from God's mercy to send down a sign.

Then His saying: ﴿I am only a clear warner﴾ means: the sign is with God; whether He sends it down or does not send it down, it does not concern me. I am only a warner, and I have no authority over Him in anything. Then, after clarifying the falsity of their doubt from one aspect, He clarified its falsity from another aspect, and said, in effect: Suppose that the sending down of a sign is a condition; nonetheless, it already exists in the Book itself.

[Then Allah the Exalted said: (Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed, in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe. Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — it is they who are the losers.")]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them?﴾ That is: if the sending down of a sign were a condition, then only the sending down of one sign would be required, and it has been sent down, which is the Qur'an, for it is a clear and lasting miracle. His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them?﴾ is an expression indicating that the Qur'an is a sign beyond what is sufficient. This is because when a speaker says, "Is it not sufficient for the wrongdoer that he is not beaten, so that he should expect honor?", it indicates that leaving him unbeaten is a great favor toward him. Likewise is His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book?﴾ And this is because the Qur'an is a miracle more complete than every miracle that preceded it, for several reasons:

The first of them: that those miracles existed only for as long as they lasted. The turning of the staff into a serpent and the raising of the dead no longer leave us any trace of them. So if there were no one who believed in the books of Allah and denied the occurrence of these things, it would be impossible to establish them without the Book. As for the Qur'an, it remains; if someone denies it, we say to him, "Then produce a sign like it."

The second: the turning of the staff into a serpent happened in one place, and whoever was not in that place did not see it. As for the Qur'an, it has reached East and West, and everyone has heard it. Here is a subtle point: the signs of the Prophet ﷺ were not things restricted to one place rather than another, because among them was the splitting of the moon, which covers the earth, since an eclipse, when it occurs, covers everywhere. This is because his prophethood was universal and not restricted to one region rather than another. The lake of Sawah dried up in one region, the Iwan of Kisra collapsed in one region, and the church of the Romans was demolished in another region, as a declaration that a general matter would occur.

The third: apart from this miracle, the stubborn disbeliever says that it is sorcery performed by means of a medicine, but this claim cannot be made about the Qur'an.

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, in that is mercy﴾, as an indication that We made it a miracle, a mercy upon the servants, so that by it they might know the truthful. This is because we have explained that the manifestation of a miracle at the hands of the truthful is a mercy from Allah. Had He not manifested it, the creation would remain in the predicament of either denying the truthful or affirming the liar, for the Prophet would not be distinguished from the pretender without a miracle. But Allah does what He wills and decrees what He intends. His saying ﴿and a reminder﴾ is an indication that it is a lasting miracle by which everyone who exists, as long as time remains, is reminded.

* * *
Then He the Exalted said: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, meaning this mercy is specific to the believers, because the miracle was a wrath upon the disbelievers, since it cut off their excuses and nullified their denial.
* * *
Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you"﴾. When his message became manifest and his proof dazzled, and the stubborn among the People of the Book did not believe in him, he said, as the truthful say when they are denied, and he brought everything that indicates his truthfulness yet was not believed: "Allah knows my truthfulness and your denial, O stubborn one, and He is witness to what I say, judging between me and you." All of that is a warning and a threat, which conveys confirmation and emphasis. Then He explained that He is sufficient by His being knowledgeable of all things. He said: ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Here there is a question: Allah the Exalted said at the end of al-Ra'd, ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43], where He placed the testimony of the People of the Book last, but in this surah He placed it first, where He said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book believe in it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 47], and among them are those who believe in it, that is, among the People of the Book. We say: the discourse there is with the polytheists, so they were argued against by the testimony of others. Then the testimony of Allah is stronger in binding them than the testimony of other than Allah. Here the discourse is with the People of the Book, and a person's testimony against himself is his acknowledgment, which is the strongest proof against him; so He put first what is more binding upon them.
Then, when the Exalted explained the two paths in guiding the two groups, the polytheists and the People of the Book, He returned to a speech encompassing both and a general warning, and said: ﴿And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — it is they who are the losers﴾, that is, those who believed in other than Allah, because other than Allah is falsehood, since it perishes, by His saying: ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. Everything that perishes has passed away, so everything perishing is false, and everything other than Allah is false. Whoever believes in other than Allah has believed in falsehood. There are issues in this:

The first issue: His saying ﴿it is they who are the losers﴾ implies restriction, meaning whoever brings belief in falsehood together with disbelief in Allah is a loser. So whoever brings one of them without the other should not be a loser. We say: it is impossible that one who brings one of them would not be bringing the other. As for the one who brings belief in other than Allah, it is because he has associated with Allah, making other than Allah like Him; yet the other is incapable, ignorant, contingent, and false, so Allah would be likewise, and this becomes a denial of Allah and disbelief in Him. As for the one who disbelieves in Him and denies Him, he would be saying that the world has no creating god, so the existence of the world is from itself, and he would thus be saying that the world is necessary, and the necessary is a god, and so he would be saying that other than Allah is a god, and this becomes an affirmation of other than Allah and belief in it.

The second issue: if belief in other than Allah is disbelief in Him, then everyone who believes in falsehood has disbelieved in Allah. Is there then any benefit in this conjunction beyond emphasis, as in the speaker's saying, "Stand up and do not sit, come near to me and do not go far"? We say: yes, there is a benefit beyond it, namely that He mentioned the second to explain the ugliness of the first, like the speaker's saying, "Do you speak falsehood and leave the truth?", to show that speaking falsehood is ugly.

The third issue: does this include the People of the Book, that is, did they believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah? We say yes, because when it was established to them that the miracle of the Prophet was from Allah, and they were certain of it, yet they were stubborn and said it was from other than Allah, they are like one who sees a person throwing stones and says, "The thrower of the stones is Zayd," and is certain that he is saying this person is Zayd, so that even if he were asked about that very person and it was said to him, "Who is this man?", he would say, "Zayd." Likewise, when they were certain that the manifester of the miracle was Allah, and they said that Muhammad was the manifester of it, it necessarily follows that they must say Muhammad is Allah the Exalted, and this is belief in falsehood. And if they say that the one who manifested the miracle is not a god, though they were certain of the specific manifester, then they would be saying that this specific one, who is Allah, is not a god, and this is disbelief in Him. This does not apply to us regarding one who says, "Perhaps the servant is created by Allah the Exalted, or created by the servant," for he too attributes the act of Allah to another, just as the miracle is an act of Allah, and they attributed it to another; this is because this speaker is ignorant of the attribution. He is like one who sees stones being thrown but does not see the thrower's person, and so supposes the thrower is Zayd and says, "Zayd is the thrower of these stones." Then if he sees the thrower with his own eyes, and he is not Zayd, he would not be certain to say, "He is Zayd." But if he sees his person and his throwing of the stones and says, "The thrower of the stones is Zayd," he is certain to be saying, "This man is Zayd." The difference thus becomes clear, in that they were stubborn, knowing that Allah is the manifester of that miracle, yet they say it is from other than Allah.

Then His saying ﴿it is they who are the losers﴾ is likewise with the most complete aspects of loss. This is because one who loses the capital and is not burdened with debts that he is pursued for is different from one who loses the capital and is burdened with those debts. When they worshipped other than Allah, they spent their lives and received in return nothing at all of benefit, and there accumulated upon them the debts of abandoning obligations, for which they will be pursued, with no capacity to bear them.

[Then Allah the Exalted said: (Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed, in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe. Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you. He knows what is in the heavens and the earth. And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — it is they who are the losers.")]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them?﴾ That is: if the sending down of a sign were a condition, then only the sending down of one sign would be required, and it has been sent down, which is the Qur'an, for it is a clear and lasting miracle. His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them?﴾ is an expression indicating that the Qur'an is a sign beyond what is sufficient. This is because when a speaker says, "Is it not sufficient for the wrongdoer that he is not beaten, so that he should expect honor?", it indicates that leaving him unbeaten is a great favor toward him. Likewise is His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book?﴾ And this is because the Qur'an is a miracle more complete than every miracle that preceded it, for several reasons:

The first of them: that those miracles existed only for as long as they lasted. The turning of the staff into a serpent and the raising of the dead no longer leave us any trace of them. So if there were no one who believed in the books of Allah and denied the occurrence of these things, it would be impossible to establish them without the Book. As for the Qur'an, it remains; if someone denies it, we say to him, "Then produce a sign like it."

The second: the turning of the staff into a serpent happened in one place, and whoever was not in that place did not see it. As for the Qur'an, it has reached East and West, and everyone has heard it. Here is a subtle point: the signs of the Prophet ﷺ were not things restricted to one place rather than another, because among them was the splitting of the moon, which covers the earth, since an eclipse, when it occurs, covers everywhere. This is because his prophethood was universal and not restricted to one region rather than another. The lake of Sawah dried up in one region, the Iwan of Kisra collapsed in one region, and the church of the Romans was demolished in another region, as a declaration that a general matter would occur.

The third: apart from this miracle, the stubborn disbeliever says that it is sorcery performed by means of a medicine, but this claim cannot be made about the Qur'an.

Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, in that is mercy﴾, as an indication that We made it a miracle, a mercy upon the servants, so that by it they might know the truthful. This is because we have explained that the manifestation of a miracle at the hands of the truthful is a mercy from Allah. Had He not manifested it, the creation would remain in the predicament of either denying the truthful or affirming the liar, for the Prophet would not be distinguished from the pretender without a miracle. But Allah does what He wills and decrees what He intends. His saying ﴿and a reminder﴾ is an indication that it is a lasting miracle by which everyone who exists, as long as time remains, is reminded.

* * *
Then He the Exalted said: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, meaning this mercy is specific to the believers, because the miracle was a wrath upon the disbelievers, since it cut off their excuses and nullified their denial.
* * *
Then He the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you"﴾. When his message became manifest and his proof dazzled, and the stubborn among the People of the Book did not believe in him, he said, as the truthful say when they are denied, and he brought everything that indicates his truthfulness yet was not believed: "Allah knows my truthfulness and your denial, O stubborn one, and He is witness to what I say, judging between me and you." All of that is a warning and a threat, which conveys confirmation and emphasis. Then He explained that He is sufficient by His being knowledgeable of all things. He said: ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Here there is a question: Allah the Exalted said at the end of al-Ra'd, ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as Witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43], where He placed the testimony of the People of the Book last, but in this surah He placed it first, where He said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book believe in it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 47], and among them are those who believe in it, that is, among the People of the Book. We say: the discourse there is with the polytheists, so they were argued against by the testimony of others. Then the testimony of Allah is stronger in binding them than the testimony of other than Allah. Here the discourse is with the People of the Book, and a person's testimony against himself is his acknowledgment, which is the strongest proof against him; so He put first what is more binding upon them.
Then, when the Exalted explained the two paths in guiding the two groups, the polytheists and the People of the Book, He returned to a speech encompassing both and a general warning, and said: ﴿And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — it is they who are the losers﴾, that is, those who believed in other than Allah, because other than Allah is falsehood, since it perishes, by His saying: ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. Everything that perishes has passed away, so everything perishing is false, and everything other than Allah is false. Whoever believes in other than Allah has believed in falsehood. There are issues in this:

The first issue: His saying ﴿it is they who are the losers﴾ implies restriction, meaning whoever brings belief in falsehood together with disbelief in Allah is a loser. So whoever brings one of them without the other should not be a loser. We say: it is impossible that one who brings one of them would not be bringing the other. As for the one who brings belief in other than Allah, it is because he has associated with Allah, making other than Allah like Him; yet the other is incapable, ignorant, contingent, and false, so Allah would be likewise, and this becomes a denial of Allah and disbelief in Him. As for the one who disbelieves in Him and denies Him, he would be saying that the world has no creating god, so the existence of the world is from itself, and he would thus be saying that the world is necessary, and the necessary is a god, and so he would be saying that other than Allah is a god, and this becomes an affirmation of other than Allah and belief in it.

The second issue: if belief in other than Allah is disbelief in Him, then everyone who believes in falsehood has disbelieved in Allah. Is there then any benefit in this conjunction beyond emphasis, as in the speaker's saying, "Stand up and do not sit, come near to me and do not go far"? We say: yes, there is a benefit beyond it, namely that He mentioned the second to explain the ugliness of the first, like the speaker's saying, "Do you speak falsehood and leave the truth?", to show that speaking falsehood is ugly.

The third issue: does this include the People of the Book, that is, did they believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah? We say yes, because when it was established to them that the miracle of the Prophet was from Allah, and they were certain of it, yet they were stubborn and said it was from other than Allah, they are like one who sees a person throwing stones and says, "The thrower of the stones is Zayd," and is certain that he is saying this person is Zayd, so that even if he were asked about that very person and it was said to him, "Who is this man?", he would say, "Zayd." Likewise, when they were certain that the manifester of the miracle was Allah, and they said that Muhammad was the manifester of it, it necessarily follows that they must say Muhammad is Allah the Exalted, and this is belief in falsehood. And if they say that the one who manifested the miracle is not a god, though they were certain of the specific manifester, then they would be saying that this specific one, who is Allah, is not a god, and this is disbelief in Him. This does not apply to us regarding one who says, "Perhaps the servant is created by Allah the Exalted, or created by the servant," for he too attributes the act of Allah to another, just as the miracle is an act of Allah, and they attributed it to another; this is because this speaker is ignorant of the attribution. He is like one who sees stones being thrown but does not see the thrower's person, and so supposes the thrower is Zayd and says, "Zayd is the thrower of these stones." Then if he sees the thrower with his own eyes, and he is not Zayd, he would not be certain to say, "He is Zayd." But if he sees his person and his throwing of the stones and says, "The thrower of the stones is Zayd," he is certain to be saying, "This man is Zayd." The difference thus becomes clear, in that they were stubborn, knowing that Allah is the manifester of that miracle, yet they say it is from other than Allah.

Then His saying ﴿it is they who are the losers﴾ is likewise with the most complete aspects of loss. This is because one who loses the capital and is not burdened with debts that he is pursued for is different from one who loses the capital and is burdened with those debts. When they worshipped other than Allah, they spent their lives and received in return nothing at all of benefit, and there accumulated upon them the debts of abandoning obligations, for which they will be pursued, with no capacity to bear them.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment. Had there not been a term appointed, the punishment would have come upon them. And it will surely come upon them suddenly, while they do not perceive.﴾

When God warned them of loss, which is the most complete form of warning, because whoever suffers loss gains nothing of benefit in return for the measure of the loss; otherwise the loss would not be that measure but less than it. An example: if one of ten people loses a dirham, it should not be that he gains in return for the dirham something worth half a dirham, for otherwise the loss would not be a dirham but half a dirham. So when they lost their lives, no benefit of lightening the punishment is attained for them, for otherwise that portion of their life would have a benefit,

صفحة ٧٢

so the wrongdoer would have a painful punishment. So His saying: ﴿And those are the losers﴾ is a mighty threat. They said: "If there is a punishment upon us, then bring it to us," displaying their certainty that there would be no punishment. Then He answered that the punishment does not come to you by your asking, nor is it hastened by your haste, because God has deferred it for wisdom and mercy. Because He is Wise, He is not changeable or fluctuating; and because He is Merciful, He is not wrathful or agitated. Had it not been for that appointed term which His wisdom required and His mercy approved, He would have no mercy and no wisdom, and would then be wrathful and fluctuating, and would be affected by your haste and changed by your request, and so would hasten. But it is not so; He does not bring the punishment upon you while you ask Him, and He does not avert the punishment from you when you seek refuge from it, as God Most High said: ﴿Every time they wish to leave it out of distress, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Hajj: 22].
* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿And it will surely come upon them suddenly﴾. The exegetes differed concerning it. Some of them said: the punishment will surely come upon them suddenly, because the punishment is the nearest of the things mentioned, and because what they asked for was the punishment, so He said: "it will surely come upon them." Others said: it will surely come upon them suddenly, meaning the term, because what comes suddenly is the term; as for the punishment after the term, it is direct witnessing. We have mentioned that in the matter of the punishment or the term coming suddenly there is a wisdom: that if its time were known, each person would rely on its distance and his knowledge of its time, so he would transgress and sin, relying on repentance before death.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ admits of two meanings.

One of them: an emphasis on the meaning of His saying "suddenly," as one says: "I came upon him in a state of heedlessness, in such a way that he did not know," so His saying "in such a way that he did not know" emphasizes the meaning of heedlessness.

The second: it is a statement that conveys an independent benefit, namely that the punishment comes upon them suddenly while they do not perceive this matter, and they suppose that the punishment will not come upon them at all.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment. Had there not been a term appointed, the punishment would have come upon them. And it will surely come upon them suddenly, while they do not perceive.﴾

When God warned them of loss, which is the most complete form of warning, because whoever suffers loss gains nothing of benefit in return for the measure of the loss; otherwise the loss would not be that measure but less than it. So when they lost their lives, no benefit of lightening the punishment is attained for them, for otherwise that portion of their life would have a benefit,

so the wrongdoer would have a painful punishment. So His saying: ﴿And those are the losers﴾ is a mighty threat. They said: "If there is a punishment upon us, then bring it to us," displaying their certainty that there would be no punishment. Some of them said: the punishment will surely come upon them suddenly, because the punishment is the nearest of the things mentioned, and because what they asked for was the punishment, so He said: "it will surely come upon them." Others said: it will surely come upon them suddenly, meaning the term, because what comes suddenly is the term; as for the punishment after the term, it is direct witnessing.
